title: [bug] runas /trustlevel:0x20000 exits 0 and the process comes back ELEVATED - the de-elevation mechanism is wrong, not broken
description:
THE FIVE-SESSION QUESTION IS ANSWERED, by 1dq's instrumentation doing exactly what it was built to do. From the operator's real oplog, 0.5.0, 2026-08-13:

  14:15:22  app-start                     tier=full  v0.5.0
  14:16:56  relaunch-deelevated           success    trigger=user-click
  14:17:31  relaunch-deelevated-mismatch  error      direction=deelevate
            wantedTier=audit landedTier=full msSinceAttempt=34537
            uac: isGroupMember true, enableLua true, partOfDomain false,
                 lockLikely false, isElevatedNow TRUE, policyWritable true
  14:17:31  app-start                     tier=full  v0.5.0

This is OUTCOME 2 of the three the handoff listed: runas accepted the request and exited 0 (no exitCode in meta means it did not fail), and Windows started the process ELEVATED anyway. So the mechanism is WRONG, not broken, and no further instrumentation around it will say which mechanism to use instead.

RULED OUT, on evidence rather than reasoning:
- The app's own auto-elevate-on-startup path. settings.json startupMode is 'audit', and main.js:221 is the ONLY startupMode read in the entire main process - it auto-elevates only when startupMode === 'full'. There is no auto-DE-elevate path either, which was checked because it would have explained the sibling report and does not exist.
- Environment. seclogon Running, EnableLUA=1, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=5, manifest asInvoker, not domain-joined, policy key writable.

ALSO ESTABLISHED, and it corrects the operator's read: the app has NOT reached Audit Mode at all since 2026-08-07. Every app-start on 08-12 and 08-13 is tier=full. So the settings-toggle path did not 'now work' either - it showed the Restarting in Audit Mode splash, runas returned 0, and the app came back Full with the honest mismatch warning. That warning IS 1dq working; the underlying switch has never taken on this machine.

NEXT STEP IS ONE MEASUREMENT, NOT MORE CODE: test/deelevation-probe.ps1, run from an ELEVATED PowerShell. It probes three mechanisms and reports which actually drop privilege here:
  A. runas.exe /trustlevel:0x20000        (what ships today)
  B. explorer.exe's token via CreateProcessWithTokenW  (the documented way to run as the logged-on user from an elevated process; a direct call, NOT the Shell.Application COM trick that was already tried and found unreliable)
  C. a scheduled task registered with RunLevel Limited
It refuses to run unelevated, because from an unelevated shell every mechanism would 'succeed' with no privilege to drop.

Whichever of B or C comes back DROPPED PRIVILEGE is the replacement for scanner.ps1's relaunch-deelevated case.
close_reason:
FIXED in 0.5.2, by measurement rather than by another theory.

test/deelevation-probe.ps1, run by the operator from an elevated shell 2026-08-13:

  runas.exe /trustlevel:0x20000              NO RESULT (exit 1)
  explorer token, CreateProcessWithTokenW    NO RESULT (child died 0xc0000142)
  scheduled task, RunLevel Limited           DROPPED PRIVILEGE
                                             Medium Mandatory Level, S-1-16-8192

runas /trustlevel is the Windows-DOCUMENTED mechanism for this exact operation and it does not work on this machine. In the app it did something worse than fail: it exited 0, so the app reported a successful de-elevation and came back Full Mode. That is why five sessions found nothing - the mechanism was not erroring, it was lying, and every layer above it faithfully reported the lie.

FIX: scanner.ps1 gains Invoke-DeelevatedViaScheduledTask, which registers a task with -RunLevel Limited -LogonType Interactive, starts it, waits for a new process, and unregisters in a finally. relaunch-deelevated calls it FIRST; runas remains as a fallback because it is documented and may work where SAFER policy is intact, but it no longer gets the benefit of the doubt.

A LAUNCH IS NO LONGER A SUCCESS UNTIL A PROCESS EXISTS. Both mechanisms now call Wait-ForNewProcess and report the PID. An exit code proved nothing - that is exactly how this survived - and is not accepted as evidence by either path.

TWO THINGS THAT WOULD HAVE BITTEN LATER, both asserted:
- ExecutionTimeLimit is [TimeSpan]::Zero (unlimited). The DEFAULT is 72 hours, after which Task Scheduler would terminate Vanish out from under someone who left it open.
- The task is always unregistered. A leftover task would show in the user's Task Scheduler as something Vanish installed, which is the residue this app exists to object to. Asserted to be gone after both the success and failure paths.

THE RECORD NOW SAYS WHICH MECHANISM RAN. The 14:17:31 entry said only 'success'. Both the relaunch-intent marker and the oplog now carry method, newPid, and on total failure the reason from BOTH attempts rather than only the last.

VERIFIED: test/deelevation-mechanism-verify.ps1 20/20; the launch path is exercised for real (registering a task for your own user needs no elevation, so it launches and returns a live PID even unelevated, and leaves no task behind). Full suite 691 passed, 0 failed. Packaged scanner.ps1 sha256-identical to source and carries the new mechanism.

REMAINING, and it is the operator's to confirm: that the de-elevated instance comes up in Audit Mode with a visible window. The probe proved the process runs at Medium integrity; only a round trip proves Vanish paints its UI from there.

title: De-elevation reports success without verifying it happened - the round trip never reached Audit Mode
description:
FIRST HARD EVIDENCE in four sessions of investigation, from the operator's round trip on 2026-08-13. It falsifies both standing theories, including mine.

THE OPLOG, verbatim:
  04:30:55  app-start              tier=full
  04:35:50  relaunch-deelevated    outcome=success  tier=full   (user clicked Restart now)
  04:37:20  app-start              tier=FULL                    <- came back ELEVATED
  04:37:29  relaunch-deelevated    outcome=success  tier=full   (tried again)

There is NO relaunch-elevated entry on 2026-08-13 at all.

WHAT THIS MEANS: the failure is not re-elevation. It is DE-elevation. The app never reached Audit Mode, so there was never anything to re-elevate and the 'Restart as administrator' button was never even on screen - it does not render in Full Mode. The operator's read ('it didnt reelevate') and my own framing were both describing a symptom one step downstream of the actual fault.

ROOT CAUSE, in scanner.ps1's relaunch-deelevated case:

    $null = Start-Process -FilePath 'runas.exe' -ArgumentList @('/trustlevel:0x20000', $commandLine) -ErrorAction Stop
    @{ success = $true }

success=true means 'runas.exe was launched'. It does NOT mean a de-elevated Vanish started. runas.exe's exit code is never captured, its stdout/stderr goes to a console window that closes immediately, and Start-Process without -Wait returns as soon as the process is created. Every failure mode of runas itself is therefore invisible and reported as success. This is the same class of defect 6lg was built to catch for the elevation direction - and 6lg only instruments THAT direction, so the mirror case had no detection at all.

ENVIRONMENT RULED OUT on this machine, so this is app code, not Windows:
  seclogon (Secondary Logon, which runas.exe requires): Running
  EnableLUA=1, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=5, PromptOnSecureDesktop=1 - normal
  package.json requestedExecutionLevel: asInvoker - Windows is not force-elevating it
  settings.json startupMode: 'audit' - the startup auto-elevate path requires 'full' and did not fire

THE FIX, which is the operator's own instinct ('should we try to get the state of elevation every time') and the answer is yes:

1. Capture the outcome, not the launch. runas.exe must be run so its exit code and error text are readable, and a non-zero exit must be reported as a failure with the real reason instead of success.
2. Bidirectional intent verification. 6lg writes an elevation-attempt marker and compares tier on the next boot; do the same for de-elevation. Every relaunch records the tier it INTENDED, and the next launch compares intent against reality and surfaces a mismatch either direction.
3. State the tier transition honestly in the UI at the moment it fails, rather than relaunching into a silent contradiction.

Filed P0 because it makes a shipped, operator-facing control (the startup-elevation toggle's Restart now) claim it worked when it did not - the precise class of dishonesty this app exists to avoid.
design: Do NOT fix by guessing at runas alternatives again. dtd already burned one attempt on Shell.Application that looked right and failed live. The durable fix is verification: whatever mechanism drops privilege, the app must confirm the resulting tier and say so when it does not match. Build the verification FIRST, then diagnose runas with it in place - the verification is what makes the next attempt conclusive instead of another guess.
acceptance_criteria: A de-elevation that does not result in an Audit Mode launch is reported to the user as a failure with the reason, and logged as a mismatch; a de-elevation that succeeds is silent. Same for elevation. Both directions covered by tests.
close_reason:
Detection and honest reporting shipped. The runas mechanism itself is NOT yet proven fixed - that needs one more operator round trip - but the app can no longer claim a tier switch happened when it did not, which was the actual defect.

WHAT CHANGED:
1. scanner.ps1 relaunch-deelevated: was Start-Process without -Wait, reporting success the moment runas.exe existed as a process. runas then ran, and whatever it decided went to a console window that closed. Now -Wait -PassThru with stdout/stderr redirected: a non-zero exit is a failure carrying runas's own reason, and success means exit code 0 rather than 'a process was created'.
2. main.js: the relaunch intent marker now records its DIRECTION, and the next boot compares the tier it landed in against the tier that direction wanted. 6lg only ever asked 'did we ask to elevate and land in Audit', so the mirror case had no detection at all - which is exactly why two failed de-elevations on 2026-08-13 produced no evidence anywhere. Logged as relaunch-deelevated-mismatch with wantedTier/landedTier.
3. renderer/core.js: a message for the de-elevation direction ('reported success but this session started with them anyway - nothing was lost, you are still in Full Mode, but the switch did not take'), and the immediate failure path now shows runas's exit code and reason instead of one sentence covering every cause.

Markers written before this change have no direction field and are treated as elevations, which is what they were - tested.

Verified: npm test 565/0, 21 new assertions. The decision logic is pinned in test/elevation-intent-verify.js as main.js evaluates it, plus structural checks that catch someone reverting main.js to a single-direction test - the specific regression that kept this invisible for four sessions.

NEXT ROUND TRIP will now be conclusive either way: if de-elevation still fails, the toast names it and the oplog carries relaunch-deelevated-mismatch with the runas exit code. Environment already ruled out on this machine: seclogon Running, EnableLUA=1, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=5, manifest asInvoker, startupMode audit.

title: Confirm elevated-relaunch fix in the portable build
description: Operator hit a blank navy window after clicking 'Restart as administrator' from the portable exe. Root cause: attemptElevatedRelaunch (main.js) used process.execPath, which for a portable build is a temp-extracted copy that can be cleaned up mid-relaunch, racing the new elevated process reading its own resources. Fixed by preferring process.env.PORTABLE_EXECUTABLE_FILE (the stable path electron-builder sets for exactly this case), plus show:false/did-fail-load so a future failure surfaces an error instead of a silent blank window. Commit e00f252. This is a live-UAC path and cannot be verified by any automated harness in this environment.
acceptance_criteria: From the rebuilt dist/Vanish-0.3.0-portable.exe, click Restart as administrator from an unelevated launch. The elevated window shows real content, not blank. If it still fails, capture the error dialog text (did-fail-load now shows one) and report it.
close_reason: Live sandbox test, 2026-08-10 (operator): launched dist\Vanish-0.3.0-portable.exe unelevated, clicked Restart as administrator, accepted UAC. Elevated window showed the real app - sidebar, program list, everything - not a blank navy rectangle. Exactly one instance running. Confirms commit e00f252's PORTABLE_EXECUTABLE_FILE fix holds in the packaged build, not just in theory.

title: Real-data test harness: the missing gate that let all of the above ship
description:
THE PREVENTION ITEM. Every defect in this epic was invisible to a 312/312 green suite because every UI test runs against test/fixtures/stub-preload.js: ONE app, clean fields, instant responses. Real conditions - 163 apps, varied shapes, multi-second scans, partial states, Windows-component entries, scrollbars - are untested end to end.

This is not 'add more tests.' It is a second harness class that runs the real preload + real backend against the real machine, and asserts on what a user would actually see. The pattern already exists and works: several throwaway diagnostics this session (dashboard stats, the search-filter race) did exactly this and each found a real bug within minutes. They were deleted instead of kept. Make it permanent.

Must cover, at minimum, per screen: does the primary action button pass a hit test with a REAL-length list; does the screen render real data without visual breakage; does an action actually change what a rescan reports.

CRITICAL CONSTRAINT learned the hard way (see AGP-3 in the pitfalls retrospective): a diagnostic that require()s main.js also spawns main.js's real visible window as a side effect, which reached the operator's screen and confused them once already. Any permanent real-data harness must handle this explicitly - suppress the window, or run headless, or make it unmistakably not-the-real-app.
acceptance_criteria: A committed real-data harness (separate from the stub suites, runnable on demand, not necessarily in npm test's default path) that loads the real preload against the real backend and asserts per-screen: primary action buttons hit-testable with a real-length list, real data renders, actions change subsequent scan results. It must reproduce at least two of this epic's defects BEFORE they are fixed - that is the proof it would have caught them. Spawns no window that could be mistaken for the real app.
close_reason: Real-data harness landed: test/real-data-verify.js + test/fixtures/real-machine-truth.ps1. Reproduced 6 real defects before any fix - details-panel action buttons 250px below the window bottom at the app's real 1080x720 size (7oo.1), Storage renders 0 of 2 fixed drives (7oo.8), 60 of 151 registry entries never reach the renderer (7oo.3), 15 genuinely-broken entries missing from Force Uninstall (7oo.2), orphaned startup items with no control on any row (7oo.4), and a 180s context-menu scan with no progress (6g2/7oo.5). main.js gained VANISH_HEADLESS_HARNESS=1 so no diagnostic can spawn a window mistakable for the app.

title: System-component filter too broad: protects all Microsoft products, not just what Windows needs
description:
Operator, 2026-08-06: 'system installs are discouraged to touch, meaning software windows needs to survive, not every ms product. but this is just ridiculous.'

Current logic (scanner.ps1 Get-InstalledApps) skips SystemComponent=1 and ParentKeyName entries wholesale, which conflates 'Windows will break without this' with 'this happens to be published by Microsoft.' A user must be able to uninstall Office, Teams, Edge, OneDrive, Visual Studio etc. - these are ordinary applications. Only genuine OS components should carry the protected treatment.

Needs a real classification pass: what is actually load-bearing for Windows vs what is merely Microsoft-published. Per Rule 24, whatever protection remains must state WHY an item is protected, not just grey it out.
acceptance_criteria: Ordinary Microsoft applications (Office, Teams, Edge, OneDrive, VS) appear as normal uninstallable entries. Genuine OS components remain protected AND state the specific reason. Verified against the real installed list on the operator's machine (163 apps), not fixtures.
close_reason: Fixed together - all three were the same root cause. Inventory now classifies every uninstall entry (application/component/update) with a stated reason instead of dropping 60 of 151. Force Uninstall reads the same classified inventory rather than a second sweep that reapplied the old drops. Redundancy groups by product family keyed on vendor. Verified on the operator's real machine: 77 applications / 73 components / 1 update, Edge+Office+OneDrive+VSCode+WSL all ordinary applications, 1 protected entry with a reason, 0 false-positive broken entries, detection proven with a planted HKCU entry, 4 real redundancy groups down from 6. npm test 312/0.

title: Force Uninstall: lists wrong/un-actionable entries and omits real ones
description:
Operator, 2026-08-06: 'force uninstall simply shows wrong entries which cant be uninstalled, still not displaying all entries.'

Two distinct defects in one surface: (a) false positives - entries listed as force-uninstallable that cannot actually be acted on, (b) false negatives - genuinely broken entries missing from the list. The detection heuristic in scanner.ps1 Find-BrokenEntries needs re-derivation against real registry state, not the planted fixtures test/force-verify.ps1 uses (19/19 passing against fixtures - see the epic's root cause).

Related: vanish-uninstaller-1qp (REQ-20 VM acceptance) is the same surface; likely resolve together.
acceptance_criteria: On the operator's real machine: every entry listed is genuinely broken AND genuinely actionable (force-uninstall completes and the entry leaves Programs and Features). Every genuinely broken entry present on the machine appears in the list. Verified against real registry state, not planted fixtures.
close_reason: Fixed together - all three were the same root cause. Inventory now classifies every uninstall entry (application/component/update) with a stated reason instead of dropping 60 of 151. Force Uninstall reads the same classified inventory rather than a second sweep that reapplied the old drops. Redundancy groups by product family keyed on vendor. Verified on the operator's real machine: 77 applications / 73 components / 1 update, Edge+Office+OneDrive+VSCode+WSL all ordinary applications, 1 protected entry with a reason, 0 false-positive broken entries, detection proven with a planted HKCU entry, 4 real redundancy groups down from 6. npm test 312/0.

title: Uninstall wizard: action buttons partially occluded by another element
description:
Operator, 2026-08-06: 'opening an item to uninstall results in poor ui, where the choice buttons are partially hidden behind another element.'

CRITICAL CONTEXT: test/ui-interaction-verify.js exists specifically to catch this class of bug (its own header documents a prior occlusion defect where 'buttons rendered perfectly and did nothing'), and it PASSES green. So the existing hit-test coverage does not reproduce the real condition - likely because the fixture renders 1 app in a short list while real data renders 163 with a scrollbar, different container heights, and a details sidebar in a different state. Reproduce with real data first, then fix, then extend the hit-test suite so the REAL geometry is covered, not just the fixture's.

Files: index.html wizard screens, index.css (.wizard-*, z-index/stacking), renderer.js showScreen().
acceptance_criteria: With the real app and real data loaded (163 apps), every wizard action button on every wizard screen passes a document.elementFromPoint hit test at its own centre. Regression test reproduces the real layout condition (list long enough to scroll, details sidebar open), not the 1-app fixture.
close_reason: Root cause was not the wizard: the details panel scrolled as a whole while its two action buttons relied on margin-top:auto, so with real registry paths the buttons rendered at y=969/1036 in the app's own 1080x720 window - 250px below the bottom edge. Fixed by making the info list the scrolling element and the actions structure, with panel chrome sized in vh. Verified by test/real-data-verify.js at 800x600, 1080x720 and 1440x900. Wizard footer buttons themselves were sound at every screen once the harness stopped mistaking Audit Mode's deliberate pointer-events:none for occlusion.

title: EPIC: Shipped surfaces are aesthetic shells - make every existing screen actually work
description:
Operator audit 2026-08-06, verbatim verdict: 'we have an aesthetic product with poor UX and minimal functionality, this is the worst of all worlds. implode the fluff, build a robust software.'

ROOT CAUSE (agent process failure, recorded so it is not repeated): every UI test in this repo runs against test/fixtures/stub-preload.js, which returns ONE fake app with clean well-formed fields. Real state on the operator's machine is 163 apps of wildly varied shape, plus real scan latency, real partial states, real Windows-component entries. Result: 312/312 tests passing while the app is visibly broken on screen. The hit-test suite that exists SPECIFICALLY to catch occluded buttons passed green while real action buttons sit occluded in the real app. Fixture-shaped testing validated fixture-shaped reality.

Prior sessions fixed defects one-at-a-time as the operator reported them, never doing a systematic screen-by-screen pass with real data. That reactive loop is what produced an app that looks finished and is not. See D:\Depthworks\Projects\ideations\agent-verification-pitfalls\RETROSPECTIVE.md (AGP-1) - the pattern was documented twice this session and still not applied where it counted.

BINDING RULE for all children of this epic: no child may be closed on a stub-test pass alone. Each requires verification against the REAL app with REAL data (the operator's machine or the Sandbox), because that is the only environment where these defects are visible at all.

STRATEGIC CONTEXT (changes priorities): operator confirmed commercialization intent - B2B paid, personal use free. This supersedes the MS Store Convenience Edition assumption recorded on vanish-uninstaller-22n. A B2B buyer will not tolerate any defect on this list. Robustness of existing surfaces now outranks new stage scope.
close_reason: All ten original children fixed and verified against the real machine, not fixtures. Measured: context-menu scan 300s+ -> 0.7s; Storage 0 -> 2 of 2 drives; inventory 91 of 151 entries visible -> all 151 classified with reasons; uninstall actions 250px off-screen -> on screen at 800x600/1080x720/1440x900; Force Uninstall now reads the same classified inventory as the app list (detection proven with a planted HKCU entry); redundancy 6 groups -> 4 real; startup orphans 3 -> 1 real (2 were false positives from quote handling); live scan progress where there was none; Windows optional features listed (135); quarantine entries state what happens if left alone. Gate: test/real-data-verify.js 152/0 across 11 sections; npm test 314/0; geometry sweep 262/0. 7oo.11 detached as deliberate follow-up scope, not a defect.

title: SEC-1 (CRITICAL): elevated command injection via registry UninstallString in uninstall-native
description:
Found by /cso audit 2026-08-03 (TASK-18). Report: .security-reports/2026-08-03-160528.json finding 1.

main.js:247 passes uninstallString straight to node:child_process exec(), which on
Windows runs it through cmd.exe /d /s /c. The string originates in the registry:
Get-InstalledApps (scanner.ps1:56,97) enumerates
HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* and copies
UninstallString verbatim; Find-BrokenUninstallEntries (scanner.ps1:2889,2906) does
the same for the broken-entry repair flow. HKCU is writable at medium integrity.

Because a shell is attached, cmd metacharacters (&, |, &&, ^) are honoured. This
path has no Get-UninstallerTrust check, no live registry re-read, and no
executable/argument split -- all three of which lib/queue.js runOne does apply.
The Vuln 3 remediation hardened only the queue path.

EXPLOIT
1. Medium-integrity code creates HKCU\...\Uninstall\FreeVideoToolbar with
   DisplayName "Free Video Toolbar" and
   UninstallString = C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /c "net localgroup administrators
   attacker /add & powershell -enc <payload>"
2. User launches Vanish and elevates to Full Mode (documented FLOW-01 path).
3. The planted entry appears in the app list -- an entry named like adware is
   exactly what an uninstaller's user wants to remove.
4. User clicks Launch Native Uninstaller (renderer.js:902) or Scan traces ->
   Run its uninstaller (renderer.js:2682).
5. exec() spawns cmd.exe as administrator with the attacker's command line.

IMPACT
One-click local privilege escalation from medium integrity to administrator, with
a shell. Registry write plus a UI click; no memory corruption, no race.

FIX
Delete the exec() path. Change the IPC contract so uninstall-native accepts a
registryPath, never a command string, then route through the queue's pipeline:
read-uninstall-entry (live re-read + Get-UninstallerTrust) -> resolve-uninstall-args
(Split-UninstallString) -> run-uninstaller (Start-Process -FilePath/-ArgumentList,
no shell), with the trust.risky acknowledgement gate in front.
acceptance_criteria: uninstall-native accepts a registryPath, never a command string; no exec()/shell anywhere in main.js; the path re-reads the live registry, splits executable from arguments, and applies the Get-UninstallerTrust risky gate; test/security-verify.ps1 plants an HKCU entry with cmd metacharacters and asserts refusal; run-all.ps1 stays green.
close_reason: Fixed: uninstall-native now takes a registry pointer and runs read-uninstall-entry -> trust gate -> resolve-uninstall-args -> run-uninstaller (Start-Process, no shell). exec removed from main.js. UWP branch calls Remove-AppxPackage as a cmdlet via the new remove-appx action. Invoke-Uninstaller gate widened from userWritable to risky. Regression tests added to test/security-verify.ps1 (elevated) and tier-verify.js (both tiers). Suite: 164 passed / 0 failed unelevated; the new elevated assertions still need an elevated run.

title: Module 3.1 RESCUE: local-only credential scan, audit-only
description:
From HANDOFF-2026-08-21 section 3, Module 3, and named there as "the highest-value, lowest-risk thing in this document" and one of the three concrete first tasks.

Module 3 is built FIRST, before any reclaim work. The sequencing is deliberate: RESCUE BEFORE RECLAIM. A tool that cannot yet delete anything but can tell you what a delete would destroy is already the most useful thing on the machine. Dependence is earned by knowing what not to touch.

WHAT IT FINDS: files that exist on disk, are gitignored, and are therefore on no remote - key.properties, .env.local, *.jks, *.keystore, .playwright_session and the like.

THE EVIDENCE, from the real cleanup: TWO KEYSTORE PASSWORDS EXISTING NOWHERE ELSE IN THE WORLD, inside folders that a delete-and-reclone would have destroyed. Signed Android apps become unshippable without them.

AUDIT-ONLY. No deletion, no quarantine, just the report. That is the whole scope of this issue.

NO COMPETITOR HAS THIS. CCleaner and BleachBit clean; neither knows what a repo's remote does not have.

Obeys aeu: the scan must distinguish "no local-only credentials" from "could not read this tree", because the second reported as the first is exactly how it would authorise destroying the thing it exists to protect.
close_reason: Shipped as finders/local-only-credentials.finder.ps1, audit-only, 24 assertions in test/finder-credentials-verify.ps1 (verified independently by me, not just self-reported: 24 passed, 0 failed). Uses real 'git check-ignore' rather than a hand-rolled .gitignore parser, and trusts only its exit code 0/1 - never bare $?. A missing git.exe, an unexpected exit code, or an access-denied directory becomes New-Unreadable, so 'could not read this tree' can never present as 'no local-only credentials here', which is the one confusion that would let it authorise destroying the thing it exists to protect. Never calls Get-Content on a matched file: name, size and git's verdict only - a tool that prints the keystore password to solve 'you might lose your keystore password' has become the problem. Every finding is costClass 'irreplaceable' with a plain-language rebuildCost. Test-NeverTouchPath consulted on every root and candidate. Uncovered: the default-root heuristic is implemented but not exercised (tests drive explicit roots for determinism), and .npmrc/.playwright_session share the proven pattern path without their own assertions.

title: Never-touch list and the safety cases already learned
description:
From HANDOFF-2026-08-21 section 4. Three real cases where something LOOKED like waste and was not. Each cost investigation during the manual cleanup; hard-coding them means it happens once.

  - C:\inetpub looks like an unused IIS leftover and is a CVE-2025-21204 MITIGATION. Deleting it weakens the machine. Hard-code as never-touch.
  - Two Antigravity installs looked like duplication and were INTENTIONAL (agentic IDE plus a VS Code fork; one is needed to install BMAD). Never auto-flag same-name installs as redundant without asking.
  - The Flutter SDK looked orphaned and was NOT - SplitSmart is a Flutter app. Detect CONSUMERS before calling a toolchain unused.

The generalisation is the valuable part: a hygiene tool that flags by shape will flag security mitigations, deliberate duplicates and toolchains with consumers. Each needs a positive test for the thing that makes it legitimate, not an exception list that rots.
close_reason: Shipped as finders/_never-touch.ps1, built as positive tests rather than an exception list, per the issue's own reasoning. C:\inetpub is data (a published CVE-2025-21204 mitigation is a fact about Windows, not about this machine) and the refusal carries the CVE number rather than the word 'protected'; matching covers anything beneath it. Test-SameNameInstallsRedundant has NO code path returning 'redundant' - byte-identical metadata still yields needs-confirmation with evidence, because the deciding fact (does the operator use both) is not on the disk; the Antigravity case is named in the regression label. Find-ToolchainConsumers returns through the three-state contract, so 'no consumers found' and 'could not read the roots' are different answers - the Flutter/SplitSmart case. Covered by 17 assertions in test/finder-contract-verify.ps1.

title: D-1: Move to quarantine acts as Next when the leftover scan finds nothing
description:
OPERATOR-REPORTED, 2026-08-21, in HANDOFF-2026-08-21 section 1. Not yet investigated.

In the uninstaller flow, when a post-uninstall scan finds NO leftovers, "Move to quarantine" still behaves like a Next button - it advances the wizard, on a screen that has no Next button and nowhere to advance to.

Operator classification: a semantic bug. The control performs navigation it does not name, in a state where navigation is not meaningful.

LIKELY SHAPE, recorded as unverified and explicitly not a diagnosis: the wizard step advances on action-COMPLETION rather than on there-being-WORK, so the zero-result case takes the success path instead of a terminal "nothing found" state.

DO NOT FIX AS A ONE-LINE GUARD. The handoff is explicit: this is a symptom of the scanner.ps1 seam problem (5p5), and patching it leaves the class intact. Fix it by making the zero-result case a NAMED TERMINAL STATE, which makes the defect unrepresentable rather than handled.

ACCEPTANCE: a regression test that asserts the STATE, not the button.
close_reason: Fixed as a state, not a guard, per the handoff's explicit instruction. renderer/wizard.js showScreen used to read btnWizPurge.style.display = (index === 4) ? 'block' : 'none' - the button existed because of WHICH SCREEN this was, never because of what was on it. It now reads canAdvance off the decision from lib/findings.js, which has no path from a zero-finding state to canAdvance, so the control is ABSENT rather than disabled or repurposed. Two terminal states where there was one: a clean uninstall and a scan that did not finish no longer share a rendering. ACCEPTANCE MET - the regressions assert the STATE: 21 in test/findings-verify.js and 27 in test/wizard-state-verify.js (a real Electron DOM run, asserting which controls exist in each state, including that returning to has-work restores the button, so a one-way guard could not pass). Also fixed the main.js half: a failed leftover scan returned {files:[],registry:[]} and rendered as 'removed itself cleanly'.

title: Finder contract: three states - found, found nothing, could not look
description:
Binding design constraint from HANDOFF-2026-08-21, section 4. Derived from FIVE instances of one defect class in the two-day machine cleanup that produced the spec:

  A check that cannot distinguish "clean" from "could not read" will happily authorise deleting work.

The five, all real: git ownership errors read as clean; [ -d ] on a case-insensitive filesystem reporting renames already done; an unquoted search path silently skipping an entire store; $? after a pipe scoring tail instead of the command (TWICE - the second immediately before an rm -rf); and a permission-denied restore-point query reported as "disabled".

BINDING:
  1. A finder must distinguish `found nothing` from `could not look`. Three states, never two. `could not look` must NEVER reach a decider as empty.
  2. A destructive step must verify its own precondition BY COMPARISON, inside the code, immediately before acting. `cp && rm` is not enough - compare counts and bytes.
  3. Never offer an irreversible action dressed as a reversible one. Already precedent here: z3s/7v3 shipped the installer cache audit-only until the vault could genuinely put it back. Hold that line for every new cleaner.

This governs every module in the suite, so it is filed as its own issue rather than repeated in each.
close_reason: Shipped as finders/_contract.ps1. The state is COMPUTED by New-FinderResult from the evidence, never passed in - New-FinderResult has no -state parameter at all, which is asserted. There is therefore no code path producing (0 findings, >0 unreadable, state=nothing). Also shipped: Assert-RemovalPrecondition (constraint 2 - compares survivor bytes and SHA256 against the disk immediately before acting, throws rather than returning a boolean a caller can forget to check) and the mirrored Node side in lib/findings.js, which RECOMPUTES state off the wire and reports any disagreement rather than silently resolving it. 54 assertions in test/finder-contract-verify.ps1, 69 in test/findings-verify.js. Found and fixed one LIVE instance while wiring it: main.js scan-leftovers caught a failed scan and returned {files:[],registry:[]}, which the wizard rendered as 'No leftovers found - this program removed itself cleanly'. An engine crash was reported to the user as a clean uninstall, on the most-used path in the app.

title: Seam: prove finder / decider / UI-state end to end on one existing scan
description:
From docs/history/HANDOFF-2026-08-21.md (spec handoff, committed 7cc9d5d 2026-08-22). Source: D:\Ideations\vanish-dev-cleanup\VANISH-DEFECTS-AND-DIRECTION.md.

THE PREREQUISITE FOR EVERYTHING ELSE IN THAT HANDOFF. Not a refactor for its own sake and explicitly NOT a rewrite - the same document measured the codebase and answered "is Vanish too bloated" with no: ~19,310 production lines across 19 files behind a 15,078-line test suite is a healthy mid-size app.

The one structural problem it did find: scanner.ps1 is 7,870 lines, 41% of all production code in a single file. When scan, classify, decide and report share one scope, A ZERO-RESULT CASE HAS NO DISTINCT TYPE. Callers cannot branch on it, so the UI guesses. D-1 is that guess.

THE SEAM:
  1. Finders - one per finding type, returning a typed result set with an EXPLICIT EMPTY RESULT. They only find.
  2. Deciders - consume typed results, apply policy (safe / needs confirmation / never), compute REBUILD COST.
  3. UI - renders states. A zero-finding state is a NAMED TERMINAL STATE, not a step that happens to be empty.

Pick the SMALLEST existing scan and take it all the way through. Prove the shape before moving the other twenty.
close_reason: The seam is proved end to end, on the smallest existing scan - the uninstall wizard's post-uninstall leftover scan, which is also where D-1 was reported. FINDERS: finders/*.finder.ps1 register themselves with finders/_loader.ps1; each returns a typed result with an explicit empty via New-FinderResult. DECIDER: lib/findings.js consumes typed results, applies policy in one place, and computes a UI state; it never trusts the state on the wire and recomputes from evidence. UI: renderer/wizard.js derives the leftover screen from that state. scanner.ps1 grew two actions (hygiene-scan, finder-probe) and a dot-source block - the twenty-first finder will touch none of it. The zero-finding case is now two NAMED TERMINAL STATES (nothing-found, incomplete), not one empty step. Verified: 54 + 69 + 27 assertions across test/finder-contract-verify.ps1, test/findings-verify.js and test/wizard-state-verify.js, all green.

title: The IPC suites raced main.js's tier resolution with a 3-second sleep, and lost in the sandbox
description:
FOUND 2026-08-20 in the first elevated sandbox run that mattered. 1179 passed, 0 failed - and the two suites the run was started for reported NOT RUN.

system-clean-purges-4.log:
  Vanish System Clean purge round trips
  Resolved tier: audit
  This verification needs Full Mode. Re-run from an elevated shell.

The shell WAS elevated (the DONE marker records elevated: True, the PowerShell suites all resolved Full Mode, and vault-engine went 2 -> 27 assertions). vault-ipc-verify.js reported the same. startup-action-ipc-verify.js, using the same 3-second sleep, happened to win the race and ran.

CAUSE, and it is the house defect class again: main.js sets currentTier = TIER_AUDIT at module scope and overwrites it when the asynchronous check-admin returns. get-tier read before that returns 'audit' with nothing behind it, and the payload does not distinguish 'audit because unelevated' from 'audit because nobody has asked yet'. The suites waited a fixed 3 seconds - a race with an operation nobody had measured. On the dev machine unelevated it gave the right answer for the wrong reason, so it never showed.

Windows Sandbox is slower to spawn the first PowerShell than the host; the engine's own comments already record 7.6s for a cold call there.

THE PRODUCT IS NOT AFFECTED, checked rather than assumed: createWindow() runs inside the same bootstrap chain, after the tier is resolved, so no window ever renders untiered. This is a harness defect only, and adg is NOT explained by it.

FIXED by using what main.js already exports for exactly this. main.js:130 says so in as many words: 'Exposed so a harness that require()s this file can wait for bootstrap - tier resolution in particular - instead of guessing with a sleep.' All three suites now 'await main.bootstrapped'. real-data-verify.js was already doing it.

STILL UNPROVEN as a result: the phase4-ipc round trip for 0wa (quarantine a cached installer, restore it byte-identical into %SystemRoot%\Installer) and the vault IPC suite. Both need one more elevated run.
close_reason: PROVEN 2026-08-20 in an elevated Windows Sandbox run. Both suites that had reported NOT RUN now run: Vault IPC 35 passed 0 failed, System Clean purges 43 passed 0 failed. Awaiting main.bootstrapped instead of a 3-second sleep is deterministic and the race is gone. Total 1320 passed, 0 failed, no NOT RUN lines anywhere in the summary.

title: z3s open half: the narrow protected-restore exception, and 7v3 unlocked
description:
OPERATOR DECISION 2026-08-19: yes - a restore may write into a protected location when the destination is the file's own recorded original path.

IMPLEMENTED, but NOT as worded, and the difference is the whole design. The restore loop's own comment says why: 'The manifest is user-writable; the restore runs elevated. Both the source it reads and the destination it writes are untrusted.' 'Restore it to where we took it from' is a claim the MANIFEST makes. An attacker who can write entry.json sets originalPath to System32\evil.dll, supplies a payload, and asks an elevated process to move it there. The literal decision is an EoP primitive with a comment explaining why it is fine.

SHIPPED SHAPE - Test-RestorableProtectedPath, four conditions, all checked against BOTH the literal path and the junction-resolved one:
  1. Directly in %SystemRoot%\Installer. Parent must EQUAL the root, not merely start with it - StartsWith would accept Installer\..\System32.
  2. Extension .msi or .msp.
  3. THE LOAD-BEARING ONE: the vault's data directory must currently pass Test-VanishDataDirAcl (protected, no non-admin writer, trusted owner). If the manifest is user-writable the recorded original path is attacker-controlled and the exception does not apply at all. Asked of the SAME function SEC-3 uses, not a copy of its reasoning.
  4. Restore only (-MustNotExist): nothing may already be at the destination. Putting back a file that is gone is a restore; overwriting one that is there is a different act.

NOT unlocked: System32, SysWOW64, WinSxS, INF, Boot, any Start Menu, any drive root, the engine's own directory.

z3s SYMMETRY PRESERVED: the quarantine guard asks the same predicate, so the vault still refuses to TAKE what restore would refuse to RETURN. Both call one function.

7v3 IS NOW REMOVABLE. dead-reference-verify on this host: 29 orphaned installers, every one offered, every one a .msi/.msp in the cache, 136.8 MB reclaimable reversibly (was 'identified but NOT reclaimable').

TESTS. security-verify gains 13 assertions incl. the untrusted-directory refusal asserted FIRST, because every other assertion in that block passes trivially on a machine where condition 3 is false - the allow half SKIPs unelevated with that reason stated. phase4-ipc-verify's 7v3 leg was inverted from 'refuses to take it' to the full round trip: purge, gone from the cache, restore, back at the original path, SHA256 byte-identical, plus a .exe planted in the same directory that is still refused before anything moves.

Host 1055/0 unelevated. The round trip and the allow half are elevated-only and run in the sandbox.
notes:
2026-08-20 SANDBOX RESULT, elevated (68A2CEC3-7F31-4).

PROVEN - the predicate, 13 assertions in security-regressions, all passing with the fixture KNOWN trusted rather than trivially:
  the installer cache is still a protected location - the exception does not un-protect it
  a .msi that is not there can be put back into it, which is the whole decision
  a .msp too
  still refused: System32 / SysWOW64 / WinSxS / the Windows directory / wrong extension / a subdirectory / a traversal back out / a drive root / the all-users Startup folder
And the two that make the rest mean anything: a freshly created vault directory is NOT trusted, and while it is not, even the one allowed location is refused.

NOT PROVEN - the end-to-end round trip in phase4-ipc-verify (purge a cached installer, restore it byte-identical to %SystemRoot%\Installer). That suite reported NOT RUN because of jmi, the tier race, not because of anything in this change. Needs one more elevated run.

Two skips in the sandbox, both environmental and both correct: 'no cached installer on this machine to test the overwrite refusal against' and 7v3's own '0 orphaned installer(s)' - a fresh Sandbox has never installed anything by MSI, so its cache and its LocalPackage reference set are both empty. The overwrite refusal and the real 136.8 MB are host facts.

7v3's offer assertions DID run there and pass: every finding removable, every one a .msi/.msp in the cache, every note still naming the protected Windows folder.
2026-08-20, SECOND elevated sandbox run (68A2CEC3-7F31-4, 17:45-17:59). 1320 passed, 0 failed.

PROVEN: the predicate, 14 assertions in security-regressions with the fixture KNOWN trusted - the cache is still protected, a .msi and a .msp that are not there can be put back into it, and System32 / SysWOW64 / WinSxS / the Windows directory / a wrong extension / a subdirectory / a traversal / a drive root / the all-users Startup folder are all still refused.

STILL NOT PROVEN, and this is not the tier race any more - jmi is fixed and the suite RAN this time. The round trip SKIPPED, for an environmental reason that will recur on every fresh sandbox forever:

  7v3 orphaned installer cache: purge -> quarantine -> restore
    SKIP  installer-cache round trip - this machine has no readable
          LocalPackage references, so the sweep correctly finds nothing.

A fresh Windows Sandbox has never installed anything by MSI, so Installer\UserData holds no LocalPackage values, so the sweep correctly proposes nothing, so there is no finding to purge and restore. WINDOWS SANDBOX IS STRUCTURALLY THE WRONG VENUE FOR THIS ONE TEST and no amount of re-running it there will help.

THE VENUE THAT WORKS is the dev host: 76 referenced packages, 29 orphaned installers, 136.8 MB. It needs ONE elevated run - the host has UAC on with PromptOnSecureDesktop=1, so it needs a human at the consent prompt.

  In an elevated PowerShell:
    cd D:\quickhelp\vanish-uninstaller
    .\node_modules\.bin\electron.cmd test\phase4-ipc-verify.js

That single suite carries both remaining unknowns: this round trip, and 5l0's PATH byte-identity at the IPC boundary.

ALSO FIXED THIS SESSION because of what this exposed: run-all.ps1 now collects SKIP lines the way it collects FAIL lines and names them at the bottom. The run finished 1320/0 with the one leg it had been started for silently skipped - a green total that is not about what it claims, which is the house defect. Every future run now says what it did not test.
close_reason:
PROVEN 2026-08-20 by an elevated run on the dev host - the venue that actually has the fixture (76 referenced packages, 29 orphans). phase4-ipc-verify: 59 passed, 0 failed, no skips.

The round trip, in full: the finding IS offered as removable; the purge succeeds; the cached installer goes into the vault; it is gone from the cache; the restore succeeds with nothing rejected; THE FILE IS BACK INSIDE %SystemRoot%\Installer WHERE IT CAME FROM; and it is byte-identical.

The narrowness, at the same boundary: a .exe planted in the same directory is NOT quarantined (status 'failed') and is still on disk - the refusal happens before anything moves, which is the original z3s bug it must not reintroduce.

5l0's PATH byte-identity passed at the IPC boundary in the same run: 'the surviving PATH is byte-identical, including the empty element nobody asked us to remove'.

Windows Sandbox skipped this leg for a structural reason recorded in the notes above; the host is the venue and it answered.

title: A PowerShell warning inside the engine lands on stdout and breaks the single-JSON contract
description:
Diagnosed 2026-08-19 from test/logs/68A2CEC3-7F31-4/network-attribution-bfh-1.log. This is why network-verify produced no Result line in the sandbox.

The log ends:
  bfh.1 network activity read
  powershell.exe : ConvertFrom-Json : Invalid JSON primitive: WARNING.
  At ...\test\network-verify.ps1:29 char:32
  +     return ($out -join "`n") | ConvertFrom-Json

So get-network-activity emitted 'WARNING: ...' ahead of its JSON. powershell.exe sends only the ERROR stream to stderr; warning/verbose/debug go to STDOUT when stdout is redirected. scanner.ps1 sets no $WarningPreference, so any cmdlet warning anywhere in the engine is written into the JSON payload.

Not a test-only problem. main.js:454 does a strict JSON.parse(stdout) and rejects with ENGINE_BAD_OUTPUT -> the user sees "Vanish's scanning engine returned something unexpected". Every action is exposed, not just this one.

Get-NetworkActivity (scanner.ps1:2185) wraps Get-DeliveryOptimizationStatus and Get-BitsTransfer in try/catch, which catches ERRORS and does nothing about WARNINGS - the likely emitters in a Sandbox session, though the exact cmdlet is not established from the log.

Fix belongs at the engine boundary, not per call site: stdout carries one JSON document and nothing else. The engine already does this correctly for progress (stderr, behind a marker, scanner.ps1:31-37) - the preamble just never extended the rule to the streams PowerShell writes on its own.
acceptance_criteria: scanner.ps1 silences the warning/verbose/debug/information streams in its preamble so no cmdlet can write to stdout. A regression check asserts the preamble sets them. The .ps1 harnesses' Invoke-Engine reports the offending output instead of dying with a raw ConvertFrom-Json exception and no Result line.
notes:
2026-08-19: fix landed. scanner.ps1's preamble now sets WarningPreference/VerbosePreference/DebugPreference/InformationPreference/ProgressPreference to SilentlyContinue before any cmdlet can run. Every .ps1 suite's Invoke-Engine now catches a non-JSON reply and throws with the first 300 characters of what actually arrived, instead of a raw ConvertFrom-Json exception that killed the file and left no Result line.

MECHANISM MEASURED, not assumed: a child powershell.exe running 'Write-Warning; PAYLOAD' returns 'WARNING: leak|PAYLOAD' to the caller, and the same child with WarningPreference set returns 'PAYLOAD' alone. That probe is now three assertions at the top of network-verify.ps1, so if the reasoning is ever wrong the suite says so rather than the fix sitting there unexamined. Four more assert the engine sets each preference within its first 60 lines.

Host npm test 982/0, network suite 51 -> 59.

STILL UNPROVEN: which cmdlet was warning in the Sandbox. Get-BitsTransfer and Get-DeliveryOptimizationStatus are the candidates in Get-NetworkActivity and both are wrapped in try/catch, which does nothing about a warning. Not needed for the fix - the boundary is fixed for every action - but a sandbox run should now show bfh.1 producing a Result line at all.
close_reason: PROVEN in Windows Sandbox 2026-08-20, elevated. The network suite produced 'Result: 50 passed, 0 failed' - it previously died mid-file on ConvertFrom-Json with no Result line at all, which run-all reported as NOT RUN. The four preamble assertions and the three measured-mechanism assertions all pass there too. Engine stdout now carries one JSON document.

title: Set-PathEntries removes PATH entries the scanner never proposed, and miscounts what it removed
description:
Diagnosed 2026-08-19 from the sandbox logs (test/logs/68A2CEC3-7F31-4). Root cause of 3 of the 5 outstanding sandbox failures.

Find-DeadPathEntries (scanner.ps1:5397) explicitly SKIPS whitespace-only PATH elements - it filters them out before it decides what is dead, so an empty entry is never offered to the user as a finding.

Set-PathEntries (scanner.ps1:6616) drops them anyway:
    if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($trimmed)) { return $false }
so any empty element in PATH is deleted as a side effect of removing something else - an edit the user never consented to and never saw proposed.

It then reports removedCount = $entries.Count - $kept.Count, which is LIST SHRINKAGE, not 'how many of the entries you asked me to remove were removed'. main.js:1815 writes the oplog with items.removed = scopeItems.length (the REQUESTED count), so the audit trail is wrong in the other direction: the registry lost 2, the oplog says 1.

Failing assertions, both suites, sandbox only:
  [system-clean-scans-4]  exactly one entry removed
  [system-clean-scans-4]  every surviving entry is byte-identical to the original PATH
  [system-clean-purges-4] the surviving PATH is byte-identical to the original
'dead entry gone from the live PATH' passes in both, which is the tell: the requested removal worked and something ELSE also changed.

Invisible on the host because the host User PATH has no empty element. It appears in the sandbox because test/sandbox/sandbox-setup.ps1 writes "$nodeDir;$userPath" into the User PATH and $userPath is empty there, leaving a trailing ';'.

This is the handoff's recurring defect class again: a confident count that is not about what it claims to be about.
acceptance_criteria: Set-PathEntries removes only entries present in the remove list and leaves every other element byte-identical, including empty ones. removedCount counts entries actually matched and removed. The oplog records the actual count, not the requested one. Both PATH suites pass on a PATH that contains an empty element.
notes:
2026-08-19: fix landed. Set-PathEntries now removes only requested entries, keeps every other element verbatim (empty ones included), reports removedCount as entries actually matched, and adds removed[]/notFound[]. main.js records the engine's count in the oplog, not the requested one. sandbox-setup.ps1 no longer plants a trailing separator.

Regressions added, both suites, and they plant the empty element deliberately so the case exists on the host too: phase4-verify.ps1 TASK-15b and phase4-ipc-verify.js REQ-15.

GROUNDING SO FAR: the transformation was run against 6 fixtures in isolation, 14/14 (empty final element survives; whitespace-only element preserved verbatim; padding kept; case-insensitive match; duplicates both removed and counted 2; notFound reported). Host npm test 982/0, and the new scan-side assertion 'an empty PATH element is never proposed as a finding' passes.

STILL UNPROVEN: the byte-identity and count assertions sit behind 'if ($isAdmin)' and behind cleaner-purge's Full Mode gate. The host session is unelevated and system-clean-purges-4 / phase4-ipc report NOT RUN. Needs one ELEVATED npm test, or the sandbox.
close_reason: PROVEN in Windows Sandbox 2026-08-20, elevated (68A2CEC3-7F31-4). All three previously-failing assertions pass: 'exactly one entry removed', 'nothing we asked to remove was reported missing', and 'every surviving entry is byte-identical, including the empty element nobody asked us to remove'. The diagnosis was right - the writer was deleting whitespace-only elements the scanner refuses to propose, and reporting list shrinkage as removedCount.

title: Sandbox booted and silently did nothing: the .wsb LogonCommand never ran
description:
OPERATOR REPORT 2026-08-19: 'nothing happened, the sandbox started is all'. The VM booted, the folders mapped, and no PowerShell window, no npm test, no output.

THREE CAUSES, and every one of them produces THE SAME SYMPTOM - a sandbox that starts and does nothing, with no error anywhere. That is what makes this worth a P1 rather than a config tweak: Windows Sandbox reports a malformed or failed LogonCommand nowhere at all.

1. UNESCAPED AMPERSAND. The LogonCommand used the call operator (& $s), and a bare & inside XML element text starts an entity reference. The document was malformed. Sandbox mounted the folders and ignored the rest.
2. UTF-8 BOM. PowerShell 5.1's Out-File -Encoding utf8 writes one, and Sandbox parses a .wsb with a BOM inconsistently.
3. THE MOUNT RACE, which would have bitten even with valid XML: LogonCommand runs at user logon, which can be BEFORE mapped folders finish mounting. A -File pointing into a mapped folder resolves to a path that does not exist yet.

FIXED, all three: the config is written as plain ASCII with no BOM; the command is XML-escaped; and it no longer points at a file - it polls for the setup script for up to 60 seconds, runs it when it appears, and prints a red explanation naming the path if it never does. start-sandbox.ps1 now also PARSES the generated file as XML before handing it to Sandbox and throws if it will not parse, so a malformed config fails loudly on the host instead of silently in the VM.

THE PATTERN, for the third time this week: a diagnostic that can go silent. dvc was a hung suite printing nothing, frr was raw text with no recovery, and this is a VM that boots into nothing.
acceptance_criteria: A fresh sandbox launch runs the setup script and npm test unattended; a deliberately broken config fails on the host with a message rather than booting a VM that does nothing.
close_reason: Fixed and validated 2026-08-19, same session it was reported. The generated .wsb is now plain ASCII with no BOM, the LogonCommand is XML-escaped, and it waits up to 60s for the mapped folder rather than pointing -File at a path that may not have mounted yet - printing a red message naming the path if it never appears. start-sandbox.ps1 parses the generated config as XML before launching and throws on the host if it will not parse. Verified: BOM false, 0 non-ASCII bytes, document parses, LogonCommand reads back intact.

title: The vault can quarantine from a location it can never restore to (fixed; the guard is now symmetric)
description:
FOUND 2026-08-18 building 7v3. scanner.ps1's restore loop calls Test-ProtectedDestination on originalPath and refuses to write into %SystemRoot% and friends. The QUARANTINE loop did not ask the same question, so the vault would take a file out of one of those locations and then refuse, later and permanently, to put it back.

MEASURED, not reasoned: a planted orphan in %SystemRoot%\Installer quarantined cleanly, the purge reported success, the vault entry looked correct (right origin, right file row, real size), and vault-restore returned 'Rejected: refusing to restore into a protected system location' with the payload stranded in the vault. The manifest recorded meta.lastRestoreFailures=1 and left status 'quarantined'.

WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE: no shipping cleaner removes from a protected location today, so nothing exercised the pair. It only surfaced because 7v3's findings live under %SystemRoot%.

FIXED: Invoke-QuarantineItems now calls the SAME predicate before moving anything, and refuses the item with 'Refused: this lives in a protected system location, and the vault could not put it back afterwards. Nothing was moved.' Deliberately the same function rather than a copy of its list, so the two halves cannot drift.

NOT DONE, and it is a deliberate non-decision: the guard was NOT relaxed to permit restoring to a recorded originalPath. That is arguably safe - a restore to where we took it from is not an arbitrary write - and it is the only way 7v3's 137 MB ever becomes reclaimable. It is a security-boundary call for the operator, not an implementation detail.
acceptance_criteria: Quarantine refuses any path the restore path would refuse, asserted at the IPC boundary with removable forced true; the file is still on disk after the refusal.
close_reason: Fixed 2026-08-18 and proven elevated. Invoke-QuarantineItems calls Test-ProtectedDestination - the SAME predicate the restore loop uses, not a copy of its list - before moving anything, and refuses with a reason naming the restore. phase4-ipc-verify asserts it at the IPC boundary with removable forced true (what a buggy or compromised renderer would send): status 'failed', the refusal names the reason, and THE assertion it exists for - the file is still on disk, because a refusal that had already moved it would strand it in the vault forever. 53 passed, 0 failed elevated.

title: dmu's registry and service legs test the ENGINE, which by design never touches the vault - so INV-1 is unproven, not broken
description:
FROM THE ELEVATED RUN 2026-08-18. One FAIL, and it is the harness again - the same class as bkn, with a harness NOTE that made it read as the opposite: 'No vault manifest found - restore could not be proven. This is the leg dmu cares most about.'

WHAT THE TRANSCRIPT SHOWED, leg 1 of dmu:
  PASS  planted a Run value to operate on
  PASS  engine removed it (error: )
  PASS  the value is actually gone from the registry
  FAIL  a .reg manifest naming the value was written to the vault (entryId )

Note the empty entryId. The check at test/elevated-confirmations.ps1:282 is guarded by 'if ($r.entryId)', so no entryId means it never even looked.

ROOT CAUSE, read from the code: THE VAULT WRITE IS IN main.js, NOT IN scanner.ps1. main.js's 'startup-action' handler (main.js:1495-1533) calls vault.quarantine({registry:[{path, mode:'manifest-only'}]}) FIRST, returns { success:false, error:'Could not write the restore file, so nothing was changed.' } if that export fails, and only then calls runPowerShell('startup-remove-registry'). It returns { ...res, entryId: quarantined.entryId }.

scanner.ps1's 'startup-remove-registry' (scanner.ps1:6513 -> Remove-StartupRegistryValue) deletes the registry value and nothing else. That is CORRECT - the vault is not the engine's job.

The harness calls Engine 'startup-remove-registry' directly, bypassing main.js entirely. So the engine did exactly what it should, returned no entryId because it has no entryId to return, and the harness reported a missing restore manifest.

SO: the product is not broken, and it is in fact safer than the failing test implies - the manifest is written BEFORE the mutation and the mutation is refused if the manifest cannot be written. But dmu is ALSO not proven, because the layer that implements its acceptance criteria was never exercised. Leg 2 (service-manual) has the same gap and does not even assert the vault. Leg 3 (task-disable) is legitimately engine-only: main.js documents that disabling a task destroys nothing and the same button re-enables it, so there is no manifest to write.

FIX: drive 'startup-action' over IPC, which means an Electron suite like phase4-ipc-verify, not a PowerShell Engine() call. Plant the probe, call the channel, assert the vault entry exists and carries the ORIGINAL data, restore through it, compare byte for byte.

THE PATTERN, for the third time in this repo (bkn, ri6, aaw): a harness that tests one layer while its assertion text claims another, and a confident comment that made it read as a product defect.
acceptance_criteria: An Electron suite drives startup-action for registry-remove and service-manual, asserting the vault manifest is written before the mutation, that the mutation is refused when the export fails, and that a restore is byte-identical. elevated-confirmations.ps1 runs it via Invoke-Suite.
close_reason: Fixed 2026-08-18. test/startup-action-ipc-verify.js drives startup-action over ipcMain for registry-remove and service-manual and asserts the OUTCOME (a restorable vault entry exists, and the mutation is refused without one) rather than the layer that produces it, so it survives the manifest export moving. It also pins the deliberate asymmetry: task-disable writes no manifest because disabling a task destroys nothing, asserted so nobody 'fixes' it later. The misleading vault check was removed from the PowerShell leg and replaced with a note saying which suite proves that half. Two harness defects found and fixed while getting it to run elevated: it printed a 'Result:' line when refusing, which run-all.ps1 parses as a clean zero-assertion pass rather than NOT RUN; and it read get-tier immediately on whenReady, but main.js resolves currentTier asynchronously from a check-admin spawn starting at TIER_AUDIT, so it refused itself out of the first elevated run it was part of. 27 passed, 0 failed elevated.

title: Sandbox config hardcodes a repo path that no longer exists, so Windows Sandbox will not start
description:
The repo moved from 'D:\quickhelp projects\vanish-uninstaller' to 'D:\quickhelp\vanish-uninstaller' (the space is gone, which is what the operator was fighting). test/sandbox/vanish-sandbox.wsb still maps HostFolder D:\quickhelp projects\vanish-uninstaller. Windows Sandbox refuses to start on a MappedFolder whose host path does not exist, so the sandbox - which is the acceptance route for 1qp and the whole Phase 3 elevated set - is dead on this machine and nobody has noticed because nobody has run it since the move.

Fixing the literal path fixes today and rebuilds the same landmine: a .wsb carries absolute host paths by construction, so the next move breaks it again silently. Generate the .wsb from the resolved repo root instead, and keep a checked-in copy for reading.
acceptance_criteria: A launcher resolves the repo root at run time and produces a .wsb that maps it; the checked-in .wsb no longer names a path that does not exist; the sandbox starts.
close_reason: Fixed 2026-08-16. Added test/sandbox/start-sandbox.ps1, which resolves the repo root from its own location and the host's Node from PATH, generates the .wsb into TEMP and launches Sandbox - so a move cannot break it again. It refuses with a real reason when the resolved root has no package.json or Node is absent from the host, rather than letting Sandbox show its own dialog. -GenerateOnly writes and reports the config without booting the VM. Grounded: -GenerateOnly resolves repo D:\quickhelp\vanish-uninstaller and node C:\Program Files\nodejs, both Test-Path true, and the output parses as XML. The checked-in vanish-sandbox.wsb has its stale HostFolder corrected and now carries a comment saying it exists to be READ and that the launcher is the way to run it. VERIFICATION-CHECKLIST.md updated to lead with the script. No test asserts the checked-in path matches the root, deliberately: this repo is public and that assertion would fail for anyone who cloned elsewhere.

title: A hung test suite printed nothing and hung the whole elevated run: no streaming, no timeout, no catch
description:
FROM THE OPERATOR, 2026-08-14, and this is the more serious of the two findings because it is about being able to tell what is happening at all:

  'at this point, vanish opens and no other actions happen, which confuses me very much, after waiting for some time and inactivity i am forced to send you these things again and again. at least, if something is happening in the background, or user intervention is needed, some information should be displayed. nothing is happening.'

The run stopped at 'vault-ipc-verify (TASK-02/03)' with a Vanish WINDOW on screen and a blank console. Three separate defects, all in the test layer, each of which alone would have produced that:

1. NO STREAMING. The wrapper ran each suite as '& $electron ... 2>&1 | Out-String', which buffers everything until the child EXITS. A suite that never exits therefore prints nothing ever - including the lines it had already written. The operator was watching a console that could not show progress by construction.

2. NO TIMEOUT. A child that never exits hung the whole script behind it, so the legs after it (9sy, and the rpdsvc change the operator actually asked for) never ran either.

3. NO CATCH, AND A REAL WINDOW. Both IPC suites are 'app.whenReady().then(async () => { ... app.exit(); })' with no .catch(). Any throw inside leaves the promise rejected and the Electron event loop ALIVE - no output, no exit code, window still up, forever. And neither suite set VANISH_HEADLESS_HARNESS=1, so main.js created a real window and ran three Full Mode startup side effects including the auto-purge sweep against the operator's REAL vault - which main.js's own comment says a harness must never do.

FIXED, all three:
- Invoke-Suite streams every child line to the console and the transcript as it arrives, with an IDLE limit (silence) and a HARD limit (total wall clock) that are reported separately from a failure, because 'hung' and 'failed' are different findings. On a limit it kills the process and any Electron started after it, prints the last line the suite managed, and says that an on-screen window or dialog is what it is waiting for. Launches electron.exe directly, not the .cmd wrapper, so the kill actually kills.
- Both suites: VANISH_HEADLESS_HARNESS=1 (no window, no auto-purge of the real vault), a .catch() that prints the throw plus the last completed assertion and exits 1, and a 240s watchdog that names the last assertion and exits 3.
- Check() no longer returns its boolean, which was printing 32 stray True/False lines into the transcript.

STILL UNKNOWN, and this issue stays open until it is answered: WHY vault-ipc-verify stopped. It cannot be reproduced unelevated (it exits 2, 'needs Full Mode', in 20 seconds, cleanly, with no window). The next elevated run now names the last assertion it completed instead of going silent, which is what will identify it.
close_reason: ANSWERED 2026-08-18. vault-ipc-verify ran clean in the elevated run - 33 passed, 0 failed, in 8 seconds - so the 2026-08-14 hang did not reproduce under the fixed harness, twice (17:33 and 18:08 runs). The streaming, the idle/hard limits, the .catch and the watchdog all worked as designed: every suite's output appeared live, and the one suite that DID misbehave in the 18:08 run (startup-action-ipc-verify refusing itself, see 87u) was reported distinctly as 'no result line; exit' rather than going silent. The most probable cause of the original hang, stated as the most probable rather than as proven: the suite ran non-headless then, so main.js created a real window and ran the Full Mode startup side effects including the auto-purge sweep against the operator's real vault, which main.js's own comment says a harness must never do. VANISH_HEADLESS_HARNESS=1 removed all three. It cannot be proven retrospectively without deliberately reverting to a configuration that hung an operator's machine, which is not worth the information.

title: elevated-confirmations.ps1 called -ParamsJson, which scanner.ps1 does not have: every dmu/bfh.2 FAIL was the harness
description:
FROM THE OPERATOR'S ELEVATED RUN 2026-08-14 17:21. Eleven FAILs, and NONE of them was a product defect.

WHAT THE OPERATOR SAW: 'engine removed it (error: Which startup entry? No value name was given.)', 'Rejected: that is not a valid service name.', 'Which task? A task name and folder are both required.', 'Nothing was captured first, so there would be no way back. Refused.'

ROOT CAUSE, PROVEN: scanner.ps1's param block is param([string]$Action, [string]$ParamsBase64). THERE IS NO -ParamsJson PARAMETER - $ParamsJson is a LOCAL variable decoded from the base64 (scanner.ps1:11-19), and the harness conflated the two. Passing -ParamsJson to a script that does not declare it does NOT error under -File: the unmatched name and its value fall into $args and are ignored. So the engine ran with no parameters at all, every time, and refused by name - correctly.

PROOF, two independent ways, neither of which needs elevation:
1. An echo probe carrying scanner.ps1's exact param block: -ParamsJson -> ParamsBase64='', decoded='', $args holds 2 leftover items. -ParamsBase64 -> decoded = the exact JSON, $args empty.
2. End to end against the real engine: 'measure-paths' with a real file path returns {"success":true,"results":[]} via -ParamsJson and the real measurement via -ParamsBase64.

WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH A P1 BUG RATHER THAN A ONE-LINE FIX: the function carried a long comment stating that the first elevated run had PROVED the cause was the Windows command-line parser stripping quotes, and that escaping the quotes fixed it. That diagnosis was wrong and the escaping was irrelevant (the quotes arrive intact). It survived because it predicted the exact symptoms it caused. This is the repo's recurring pattern - code that diagnoses itself in a comment and then does the opposite (ri6, aaw) - and the comment being confident is what stopped anyone re-checking.

ALSO PROVEN BY THE SAME OUTPUT: the run really was elevated and the engine really did execute. Every one of those actions checks Test-IsElevated BEFORE it checks parameters (scanner.ps1:2781, 2657), and not one returned 'Full Mode required'.

FIXED: Engine() now base64-encodes exactly as main.js does (main.js:396,403). dmu and bfh.2 are still UNPROVEN - they have never actually run - and stay open until an elevated re-run passes them.
close_reason: Fixed in cf50901 (the harness now passes -ParamsBase64); re-proved end to end 2026-08-16 against the real engine at the new unspaced repo path. measure-paths over lib/ returns sizeBytes 61191 via -ParamsBase64 and {"success":true,"results":[]} via -ParamsJson - the harness bug reproduced and the fix confirmed, both unelevated. No product defect ever existed here; dmu/bfh.2's eleven FAILs were all this.

title: Decide how Vanish relates to System Informer (MIT) for CPU/RAM/process intelligence
description:
OPERATOR QUESTION 2026-08-14: 'if its foss, can we integrate it into vanish? because now even microsoft and other applications enable modernised efficiency, and an xp era software that was built in an ecosystem of bloatware may not really be as relevant anymore.'

LICENCE, VERIFIED 2026-08-14 against the LICENSE file itself rather than from memory:
System Informer (winsiderss/systeminformer, formerly Process Hacker) is MIT.
README states '100% Free Software (MIT)'. LICENSE.txt is the standard MIT text
with NO component carve-outs and NO restrictions on redistribution or bundling.
16,404 commits on master - actively maintained, not abandoned XP-era code.

THIS CHANGES THE PICTURE. CLAUDE.md's licence boundary was written against
WinDirStat (GPL-2.0) and BleachBit (GPL-3.0+), where vendoring is forbidden
because this repo is MIT and public. MIT-to-MIT has no such problem. Bundling,
vendoring source, or lifting techniques are ALL legally available here. That is
a genuinely different situation from every previous 'use existing FOSS' call in
this project, and the rule should not be applied by reflex.

WHAT IS STILL NOT DECIDED, and needs to be before any code:

1. WHAT 'INTEGRATE' MEANS. System Informer is a full GUI application, not a
   library. Realistic options, roughly in increasing cost:
   (a) Detect an existing install and hand off to it (zero bundle cost, zero
       maintenance, no duplication - the CLAUDE.md default).
   (b) Vendor specific TECHNIQUES from its source (MIT permits it) for things
       Vanish needs and Task Manager cannot answer.
   (c) Bundle the binary and launch it.
   (d) Vendor large parts of it into the engine.

2. THE KERNEL DRIVER IS THE REAL COST, not the licence. System Informer's
   deeper capabilities need KSystemInformer, a signed kernel driver. Bundling a
   kernel driver means driver signing, Microsoft attestation, conflicts with
   security products, and a much heavier install - for an app whose whole pitch
   is that it is honest and light. The userland half works without it. Anything
   past option (a) has to answer whether the driver is in scope, and the
   default answer should be no.

3. THE OPERATOR'S RELEVANCE ARGUMENT IS HALF RIGHT AND WORTH ENGAGING.
   Windows now ships Efficiency Mode, browsers sleep tabs, and the 2010-era
   'reclaim your RAM' framing really is less urgent. But System Informer is
   actively developed, so 'XP-era' describes its lineage rather than its state.
   The honest read is not that it is obsolete - it is that RESOURCE MONITORING
   is a solved, commodity problem, which is exactly the CLAUDE.md test:

     'Before proposing work, name what already solves it... and what Vanish
      adds that they cannot. If the honest answer is nothing, that is the
      finding - say so instead of building it.'

   Task Manager and System Informer both solve 'show me what is using CPU/RAM
   and let me kill it'. Vanish should not build a third one.

WHAT VANISH CAN ANSWER THAT NEITHER CAN, and the only version of this worth
building: ATTRIBUTION. Neither tool has an installed-program map, a startup
inventory, or a listener map. Vanish has all three. The sentence nothing else
on the machine can assemble is:

  'This process is using 3.2 GB. It belongs to <installed program>, which you
   have not opened since <date>, it starts automatically, and it is reachable
   from your network on port N.'

That is ddx's shape applied to resources - and ddx came from exactly this kind
of gap. The CPU/RAM numbers are the CHEAP part and are already half-present in
the Task Manager tab; the map is the asset.

ALSO PENDING FROM THE SAME MESSAGE, and deliberately NOT started: 'a mechanism
to stop such suspicious processes' plus 'an intelligence model to detect
resource hogs'. Both need a decision before code, because both sit on top of
Rule 6:
  - An automatic or semi-automatic process KILLER acting on heuristics is the
    'confident wrong answer' failure mode this project keeps fixing, but with
    teeth. Killing the wrong process loses a user's unsaved work.
  - An 'intelligence model' scoring processes as suspicious is precisely the
    scoring Rule 6 forbids. The tda amendment was scoped to GROUPING only and
    explicitly may not be widened by reflex.
  A defensible version states facts and lets the user act, exactly as ddx does.

RECOMMENDATION for the next session: option (a) plus the attribution layer.
Do not bundle, do not vendor, do not build a resource monitor. Build the join
between a running process and the installed-program map, and let System
Informer be the thing Vanish points at for deep process work.
close_reason:
DECIDED by the operator 2026-08-14: option (a) plus the attribution layer, which is what this issue recommended.

  DO:    detect an existing System Informer install and hand off to it (y1j), and build the join between a running process and the installed-program map (0bi).
  DO NOT: bundle it, vendor its source, ship its kernel driver, or build a third resource monitor.

The licence finding stands and is worth keeping: System Informer IS MIT (verified against LICENSE.txt, no carve-outs), so bundling was LEGALLY available here in a way it is not for WinDirStat (GPL-2.0) or BleachBit (GPL-3.0+), which is what CLAUDE.md's licence rule was written against. It is refused on COST, not licence: KSystemInformer means driver signing, Microsoft attestation, security-product conflicts and a much heavier install, for an app whose pitch is that it is honest and light.

And the operator's relevance argument was engaged rather than waved off: 'XP-era' describes System Informer's lineage, not its state (16,404 commits, actively maintained). The honest read is that RESOURCE MONITORING is commodity - which is exactly why Vanish should not build one, and exactly why the attribution join is the part worth building.

Follow-ups filed: 0bi (attribution join, P2 - the substance), y1j (hand-off detection, P3), qsm (the two questions from the same message that remain undecided: a process-stop mechanism and 'intelligence model' scoring, both refused by default under Rule 6).

title: [bug] GPU attribution named the wrong card - phys_N is not an adapter identity
description:
OPERATOR SCREENSHOT 2026-08-13, Vanish beside Windows Task Manager: Windows shows GPU 0 = AMD Radeon at 2% and GPU 1 = NVIDIA RTX 3080 at 13%, with dota2 on the NVIDIA. Vanish showed a single pill 'GPU 0: 20%' and dota2 at 19% wearing a RED AMD logo.

MEASURED, not reasoned about. Raw GPU Engine counters on that machine:

  luid 0x0000ed1f  phys_0  29.3%   AMD Radeon(TM) Graphics
  luid 0x0000fa2a  phys_0   0.0%   Microsoft Basic Render Driver
  luid 0x0000fa8e  phys_0  19.3%   NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Laptop GPU

THREE ADAPTERS, ALL REPORTING phys_0. phys_N is the physical index WITHIN an adapter's own group, not a global GPU ordinal, so on an ordinary machine it is 0 for everything.

Get-GpuUsageByProcess keyed byAdapter, byPid[].adapters and luidByAdapter on $physIdx.
