close_reason:
Shipped in 0.6.2/0.6.3, from the operator's direct request 2026-08-14: 'the network activity items need a stop process button per row. safety warnings issued for reasonable activities, like "normal for so and so process" which is already shown. otherwise a generic warning so people knw what they are doing. still requires elevation.'

Delivered exactly that. A Stop button per row, elevation-gated, visible-but-inert in Audit Mode with the reason like every other destructive control (REQ-04).

THE CONFIRMATION ADAPTS, which is the part that was asked for. Where Vanish already knows what the program is - the same classifyNetProgram() knowledge that prints 'normal for a web browser' beside a high connection count - it says so BEFORE asking, because that is the fact most likely to change the answer. Where it does not know, it says so outright rather than inventing a reassurance or a warning it cannot support. Every dialog states what is actually lost: unsaved work, transfers that will not resume, and that this is NOT a removal so Quarantine cannot undo it.

Two things found while building it, both operator-reported and both real:

1. BITTORRENT LOOKED IDLE. Measured on their running qBittorrent: 4 TCP ESTABLISHED (all Vanish counted), 15 TCP across all states, 21 UDP sockets. BitTorrent moves data over uTP (UDP) and finds peers over UDP DHT, so a client saturating the link showed as a near-idle process with four connections - and the list SORTED on that number, so it ranked below a browser tab. UDP and non-established TCP are now counted and shown, reported separately and never added into the connection count. A UDP row is a socket, not a conversation.

2. THE RATE TILES CLAIMED SOMETHING THEY DID NOT MEASURE. 'Download'/'Upload' read as connection capacity; they are what crossed the wire in the last sample. Now 'Downloading now'/'Uploading now', with the negotiated link rate shown separately - 866.7 Mbps link against 10.2 Mbps actual line speed on this machine, numbers with nothing to do with each other.

Capacity itself is now measurable (0.6.3) behind its own consent, against speed.cloudflare.com, chosen by the operator after being shown the trade.

VERIFIED: full suite 750 passed, 0 failed; network-verify went from 41 to 47 assertions.

title: Task Manager details pane overlaps the process table when a row is selected
description:
Operator, 2026-08-13, with screenshots at two window sizes: 'task manager lets that space on the right remain that way permanently... indicators is hidden behind that space'.

TWO defects, one fixed and one not.

FIXED (this session): the pane reserved its width permanently, selected or not. index.css .process-details was 'width: 320px; flex-shrink: 0' unconditionally, so on a wide window it was dead space and on a narrow one it stole the table's width. Now width:0 when inactive, 320px on .active. Measured at the operator's own 1110x741: details pane 0px, Indicators column right edge 1102 inside a container ending at 1110, i.e. visible.

NOT FIXED: with a row selected, the pane paints OVER the table rather than the table compressing beside it - the Indicators header renders clipped mid-word at the pane boundary. Adding min-width:0 to .process-list-container (the standard flex fix, since a flex item defaults to min-width:auto and refuses to shrink below its content) plus overflow-x:auto did NOT resolve it, so the cause is something else and was not identified before running out of session. Next session should measure the container and table widths in the SELECTED state specifically - that measurement was attempted and the instrumentation edit failed, so it is genuinely unknown rather than inferred.

WHY THIS IS THE SAME BUG TWICE, and it is worth reading before fixing: index.css:761-768 carries this comment from ri6 -

    'ri6: before any selection this panel was invisible (opacity:0) but still
     claiming its full clamp() width from the workspace, permanently squeezing
     the app list for nothing. Collapse it to zero out of the layout instead -
     scoped to the All Programs sidebar specifically, since that is what was
     reported; Task Manager's process-details panel is unchanged.'

A previous session diagnosed this exact defect, fixed one instance, and deliberately scoped the fix away from the other because only one had been reported. The operator then reported the other one. Fixing the reported instance rather than the class is what produces the impression of a project repeating itself.

FIX DIRECTION: generalise rather than special-case again. Both panels are .details-panel; the collapse-when-inactive behaviour should belong to the class, with per-panel width overrides only where the widths genuinely differ. Do not add a third scoped rule.
acceptance_criteria: At 1110x741 with a process selected: the table compresses beside the pane rather than being covered, and the Indicators column is either fully visible or reachable by horizontal scroll within its own container. Verified by screenshot at that size, not only by measurement - the measurements reported this as fine while the screenshot showed the overlap.
close_reason:
Fixed in 0.5.0, and the cause was not what the issue assumed.

MEASURED IN THE SELECTED STATE, which is the measurement the last session lost: at 1110x741 the container correctly shrank to 544px and THE TABLE STAYED AT ITS 602px MIN-CONTENT, right edge x=850 against a container ending at x=790. The pane was never painting over anything. The table was overflowing into a horizontal scroller nobody notices and the Indicators header was clipped mid-word at the container edge, which looks identical to being covered. That is why min-width:0 plus overflow-x:auto did nothing - the container was never at fault.

No single column owned the 602px: six nowrap headers plus a Process column whose content is a filename with no spaces to break at, so the one column that should have given ground could not.

FIXED AS A CLASS, per the issue's own direction:
- .details-panel:not(.active) collapses - the ri6 rule generalised off #details-sidebar. The comment that named the sibling it skipped is gone.
- .process-details now declares NOTHING about its own width. The hard-coded 320px was the last special-case and the expensive one; the class clamp gives 250px at 1110px and 340px on a wide window.
- Both tables are table-layout:fixed, so a table is exactly its container's width at any size and cannot overflow. Name columns ellipsise with the full value in a title.
- Column widths rebalanced against the narrow state; th nowrap removed (under fixed layout it can no longer widen anything, only clip); sort arrow uses a non-breaking space so it stops dropping to a second line and making every header row 17px taller.
- .process-details.active got its padding and border back. Its base rule set padding:0/border:0 and .active never restored them, so a SELECTED pane rendered with its labels flush against the glass edge - plain in the screenshot, invisible to every width measurement taken of it.

THE TEST FOUND THE SIBLING, WHICH IS THE POINT. test/details-panel-layout-verify.js tests the RULE against every .details-panel at 1110/1000/1280/1440. It immediately failed All Programs at three of four widths - the identical overflow, never seen by hand because its Name and Publisher columns are usually prose and wrap. Seed it with 'python3.11-3.11.9-amd64' and it overflows. It also found .apps-list-container missing the min-width:0 its sibling has carried for months: the same omission, a third instance, in the same file.

Also fixed here on operator request: the GPU adapter icon now LEADS the percentage instead of trailing it, and the column was widened (10% -> 14%) plus nowrap so the icon and figure always share one line - at 10% they wrapped.

Verified: 52/52 in the new suite, screenshotted at the operator's own 1110x741 with a row selected, all seven headers spelled out and nothing clipped. Full suite 660 passed, 0 failed.

title: An inferred install date renders identically to a recorded one
description:
Found 2026-08-13 by auditing our own code for the exact mistake I had just made in conversation: I read a date off an adjacent registry row and stated it as RealPlayer's install date. RealPlayer's InstallDate value is EMPTY. Vanish has a guarded version of the same move, and does not label it.

scanner.ps1:262-265

    $installDate = Format-InstallDate ([string]$key.GetValue('InstallDate'))
    if (-not $installDate -and $childName -match '^\d{8}$') {
        $installDate = Format-InstallDate $childName
    }

When a program records no InstallDate, Vanish falls back to the uninstall KEY NAME if that name is eight digits. The heuristic itself is defensible - several installers do name their key with the install date - and it is properly guarded, so RealPlayer (key name 'RealPlayer 25.0') correctly gets null rather than a fabricated date.

The defect is downstream. Both render sites treat the two identically:

    renderer/core.js:851  const dateStr = app.installDate ? app.installDate : 'Unknown';
    renderer/core.js:923  elements.detDate.textContent = app.installDate || 'Unknown';

So a date the program actually recorded and a date Vanish GUESSED from a key name are presented as the same fact, in the same styling, with nothing distinguishing them. A user sorting by install date, or deciding whether something is old enough to remove, is acting on a mix of recorded and inferred values with no way to tell which is which.

This is the app doing, in miniature, exactly what this project exists to refuse: presenting an inference with the confidence of a measurement. It is also directly analogous to bu2's owned/orphaned/unattributed distinction, which was built precisely so a guess could never wear the clothes of a fact - the same discipline simply was not applied here.

FIX: carry the provenance (recorded vs inferred-from-key-name) alongside the value and show it - a marked date, a tooltip naming where it came from, or an explicit 'approx.'. Do not remove the fallback; a probable date is more useful than 'Unknown'. It just has to admit what it is.

Worth checking the same pattern elsewhere while in here: sizeBytes has an EstimatedSize fallback in the same loop, and 'estimated' is in the variable name but may not reach the UI as a caveat either.
acceptance_criteria: A date derived from the key name is visually distinguishable from one the program recorded, and says which it is; the fallback still happens; sorting behaviour is unchanged.
close_reason:
Fixed in 0.5.0, and the audit the issue suggested found a THIRD instance the issue had not.

scanner.ps1 now carries installDateSource alongside installDate everywhere it sets one:
- 'recorded'       the program's own InstallDate registry value
- 'key-name'       the eight-digit uninstall key name fallback
- 'folder-created' a Store app's install folder CreationTime

THE THIRD ONE IS THE FINDING. c0y named the key-name fallback and flagged sizeBytes/EstimatedSize as worth checking. It did not name the UWP path, and that one is the closest match to the original mistake: the RealPlayer error was stating a FILE TIMESTAMP as an install record, and Get-InstalledUWPApps was doing exactly that, from the install folder's CreationTime, for every Store app on the machine. Now labelled.

RENDER SITES, both fixed:
- the list marks an inferred date with a quiet tilde carrying a tooltip that names where the date came from
- the details pane spells out '(approx.)' in words, because it has room for words rather than a mark the user has to decode

The tilde is deliberately quiet. The claim is 'approximate', not 'suspect' - these dates are probably right, and a warning colour on a probably-correct date is its own kind of dishonesty. Asserted: the caveat text may not contain 'unsafe/suspicious/wrong'.

A date arriving with NO source (an older engine build, or any path that never set the field) is treated as INFERRED, not silently promoted to recorded. Claiming a date is measured when nothing said so is the exact fault being fixed.

The fallbacks stay - a probable date beats 'Unknown'. Sorting is unchanged and asserted in both directions; the marker never leaks into the sorted value.

sizeBytes/EstimatedSize was checked as the issue asked and NOT changed: EstimatedSize is a value the installer itself wrote to the registry, so it is recorded rather than inferred - Windows' name for it is misleading, but Vanish reading it is not the same move. bu2's owned/orphaned/unattributed already covers the genuinely attributed-by-inference case.

Verified: test/install-date-provenance-verify.js 24/24, wired into run-all, and re-asserted against the PACKAGED app.asar. Full suite 660 passed, 0 failed.

title: Task Manager GPU column does not say WHICH GPU a process is using
description:
Operator, 2026-08-13, third time raised and now unambiguous: 'task manager - gpu column in task manager still has no indication of which gpu is being used.' Earlier sessions could not tell whether this meant the per-adapter vendor logos above the table or the process table's own GPU column. It is the COLUMN.

The data already exists and is already parsed. Get-GpuUsageByProcess reads '\GPU Engine(*)\Utilization Percentage', whose instance names are shaped pid_<pid>_luid_<hi>_<lo>_phys_<n>_eng_<m>_engtype_<type> - the adapter identity is right there in every sample, and the function already builds a byAdapter map alongside byPid. The renderer shows the summed percentage and throws the adapter away.

Scope: show which adapter each process's GPU time is on, next to the number. Where the existing LUID-to-vendor matching resolves a name, use it; otherwise 'GPU 0' / 'GPU 1', which is exactly what Windows' own Task Manager does and for the same documented reason (phys_N cannot be cheaply mapped to a friendly name, and an idle discrete GPU under hybrid graphics reports no instances at all rather than zero).

A process using both adapters must not be collapsed to one - show the busier one and indicate there is more, rather than silently picking.
acceptance_criteria: Each process row with GPU activity names its adapter; a process spanning adapters is not silently reduced to one; a machine with a single GPU does not gain a pointless column of identical labels.
close_reason:
Delivered across 0.5.0-0.5.3, and it needed three fixes rather than one because the first implementation shipped a confidently wrong answer.

What aaw asked for: the Task Manager GPU column should say WHICH GPU a process is using.

0.5.0  the adapter mark rendered, but per-process figures were dead - the byPid projection never followed aaw's own shape change and threw once per process (anz).
0.5.1  per-process figures restored.
0.5.2  -
0.5.3  the mark finally names the RIGHT card. Everything keyed on phys_N, which is not an adapter identity - three adapters on the operator's laptop all report phys_0, so they merged into one 'GPU 0' and inherited whichever LUID sorted first. dota2 on the NVIDIA wore a red AMD logo (02f). Also fixed: the chrome://gpu vendor fetch raced the page and frequently returned nothing, and the Basic Render Driver was dropped from the name map while still appearing in the counters.

Operator request folded in: the adapter icon LEADS the figure rather than trailing it, and stays an icon rather than a spelled-out vendor name - 'NVIDIA' in a column that narrow wraps and makes every row taller for a word the icon colour already carries. The column was widened and pinned nowrap so the two always share a line (5z5).

Shipped state, measured on the operator's hybrid laptop: the summary names every adapter present, a process spanning two cards shows the busier one with a +N rather than being reduced to one, and an adapter Vanish cannot name says so instead of inventing an ordinal.

title: Startup items: split killable from necessary, collapse the necessary ones
description:
Operator, 2026-08-13: 'could you categorize startup items as killable and necessary? that way necessary things could be hidden behind a collapsible section and not seen as a massive list.'

The Health Advisor startup list shows everything at once, so the handful of entries a person could act on are buried among the ones they must not touch. A long undifferentiated list reads as 'all of this is suspicious', which is the opposite of what this app is for.

Split into two groups: entries safe for a user to disable, and entries the machine depends on. The necessary group renders COLLAPSED by default with a count; the actionable group is open.

TRUST MODEL - operator direction, 2026-08-13, and this is a DELIBERATE AMENDMENT TO RULE 6, not an oversight. Rule 6 forbids a trusted-publisher allowlist. The operator has authorised one for THIS surface, with a scope they named:

  'we can trust microsoft, antivirus solutions, and highly vetted + necessary
   third party software killing which could compromise the computer's use.'

Plus a case worth reading twice, because it inverts the usual assumption:

  'this is not useful in personal cases, but is necessary for corporate/
   enterprise machines where they install legalised spyware to monitor their
   employee's activities.'

That is the sharpest reason to build this. On a managed machine, the monitoring agent is exactly the thing an employee should NOT disable - not because it is benign, but because disabling it is a disciplinary event and may break compliance. 'Necessary' here means 'do not touch this without knowing what you are doing', which is a different and more honest claim than 'this is good software'. The wording must carry that distinction: NEVER 'trusted', NEVER 'safe'. Something like 'Managed by your organisation' or 'Your system depends on this'.

CLASSIFICATION, strongest evidence first:
  1. Authenticode signature subject - Microsoft, and the major AV vendors. This is the allowlist Rule 6 previously forbade; it is now permitted for THIS grouping decision only, and it may never be used to permit or block a removal elsewhere in the app.
  2. Target resolves under %SystemRoot% or is a registered service running as LocalSystem.
  3. Enterprise-management signals: the machine is domain-joined or MDM-enrolled, the entry is under a Policies key, or it is installed machine-wide by an installer the user did not run. On such a machine, err toward NECESSARY and say why.
  4. The orphan check that already runs (exeExists=false) is the clearest KILLABLE signal there is - a startup entry pointing at a file that is gone.
  5. Whether the owning program is still in the installed-programs map (the same join bu2 uses).

BINDING: anything Vanish cannot classify goes in the ACTIONABLE group with an explicit 'no opinion' label, never hidden. Hiding what we cannot explain is how a cleaner ends up disabling something that mattered. Rule 24 also applies: 'necessary' must not render as alarming.

Worth noting the rpdsvc finding from the same conversation as a counter-example that keeps this honest: RealPlayer's service runs as LocalSystem, auto-start, and would score 'necessary' on the LocalSystem signal alone - while being software the operator does not use, listening on all interfaces. LocalSystem must therefore be a WEAK signal, never sufficient on its own.
acceptance_criteria: Startup entries render in two groups; the necessary group is collapsed with a count; unclassifiable entries appear in the visible group labelled as no-opinion rather than hidden; no trusted-publisher list is introduced.
notes: Rule 6 amendment authorised by the operator 2026-08-13, scoped to grouping only. Mirror this into docs/promptgate.md Rule 6 when implementing, with the scope limit stated, so a future session does not read the allowlist as general permission.
close_reason:
Shipped in 0.6.1.

The Health Advisor startup list now leads with entries a person can act on; the rest collapse behind a row stating its own count. On this machine: 23 visible, 18 collapsed.

RULE 6 AMENDMENT IMPLEMENTED AND SCOPED, and mirrored into docs/promptgate.md as the issue required. The publisher list decides which visual GROUP an entry is drawn in and nothing else; it may never permit or block a removal. test/startup-groups-verify.js asserts the list is referenced only where it is defined and used - if that count changes, the amendment has widened and the change should be refused.

WORDING, asserted rather than intended: the words 'trusted' and 'safe' appear nowhere in the surface. 'Necessary' means DO NOT TOUCH THIS WITHOUT KNOWING WHAT YOU ARE DOING. The managed case explains itself as policy, never as approval, and never implies the monitoring software is benign - which is the operator's corporate case handled honestly.

Anything unclassifiable is VISIBLE and labelled 'Vanish has no opinion' rather than left blank. A blank reads as approval.

THE FIRST IMPLEMENTATION FAILED EXACTLY AS THIS ISSUE WARNED, by a route the issue had not named. It treated any non-zero EnrollmentType under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Enrollments as MDM enrolment. Measured on this ordinary personal machine: 34 such keys, mostly EnrollmentType=1 with no provider, plus Windows' own Local/Cloud/Deploy Authority records. So the machine read as managed, and the 'managed machine + HKLM entry' rule swept ALL THREE RealPlayer startup entries into the hidden group, telling the operator they were placed by whoever administers the PC - about software they had asked to get rid of an hour earlier.

Fixed twice over: MDM detection now needs a real ProviderID plus a UPN or discovery URL, and 'managed' now requires the entry to sit under a POLICIES KEY. 'The machine looks managed' is a fact about the machine and says nothing about who put this particular program in Run. Evidence about the entry, not a proxy. Both are asserted.

The rpdsvc counterexample from ddx is preserved in the code and the suite: LocalSystem plus auto-start would have scored 'necessary' on that signal alone, so LocalSystem is weak and never decides alone.

VERIFIED: test/startup-groups-verify.js 23/23; rendered against the real 41-entry startup list and screenshotted with RealPlayer correctly visible and actionable. Full suite 742 passed, 0 failed. Packaged app booted from app.asar clean.

title: Cut the 1.0 release: version bump, artifact verification, tag, known-limitations note
description:
Phase 4 of docs/PRE-RELEASE.md. No release-mechanics issue existed, so the last step of the plan had nowhere to live.

Steps: npm test green; build both artifacts; verify the packaged output the way every build this cycle was verified (extract app.asar and diff renderer.js/index.html/index.css/main.js/preload.js against source, sha256 scanner.ps1 and corrections.json); version bump; CHANGELOG release section; tag; push.

Must also add a known-limitations note to the README covering the three gates waived for this release, because shipping them silently would be exactly the overclaiming this app refuses everywhere else: the binary is unsigned (SmartScreen interstitial on any machine but the operator's), there is no clean-VM pass (0xt closed), and acceptance is single-user (442 deferred).
acceptance_criteria: Artifacts built and content-verified against source; README states the three waived gates plainly; tag pushed.
close_reason:
Cut 0.4.0, not 1.0, and the distinction is deliberate: docs/RELEASING.md gates the RELEASE bump on the PRE-RELEASE ship list being done or explicitly waived, and Phase 3 (six elevated confirmations) is neither - every one needs a human at a real UAC prompt. RELEASING.md also says in as many words that a major feature completing is a MAJOR bump, not a RELEASE bump. Bumping to 1.0 here would have broken the release rule on the same day it was written.

0.4.0 qualifies as MAJOR under the stated criteria: Stage 8 (reduced) reached functional completion (zrw), a new capability tier shipped (bu2), and the IPC action interface gained new actions (snapshot-*, attribution-scan, measure-paths, install-snapshot).

Verified: npm test 544/0. Both artifacts built (Vanish-0.4.0-x64.exe, Vanish-0.4.0-portable.exe). app.asar extracted and diffed - main.js, preload.js, index.html, index.css, all seven renderer modules and every lib module IDENTICAL to source; scanner.ps1 and corrections.json sha256-identical. Then the packaged app was BOOTED from app.asar with the stub preload and asserted to resolve its cross-module functions with a clean console - that check is what would have caught the package.json 'renderer.js' omission the decomposition introduced, and it is now the standard for this project rather than a diff alone.

README already carries the three waived gates in Known limitations. PRE-RELEASE.md now carries a status table saying plainly that what stands between 0.4.0 and 1.0 is not code - it is Phase 0 and Phase 3, both of which need a person at a consent dialog.

title: Ping tile shows a bare private IP with no clue it is the user's own router
description:
Operator 2026-08-12: saw '10.128.67.147' in the tap-to-ping tile, looked it up in an external IP tool, got told it is an RFC 1918 private address with no location or owner, and reasonably asked what it is. Quote: 'a private address doesnt fill people with confidence'.

The value is CORRECT. Verified on the operator's machine: Wi-Fi adapter 10.128.67.112, IPv4 default gateway 10.128.67.147. scanner.ps1 Get-NetworkActivity reads GatewayAddresses off the adapter carrying the default route and prefers the IPv4 entry (scanner.ps1:1510-1526); renderer.js:2311 seeds pingDestination from it. Pinging the user's own router is the entire point of kp0 - it is what keeps the one permitted packet on the local network.

The bug is presentation, not data: pingTileHtml() (renderer.js:2478) renders the label as literally 'to 10.128.67.147'. Nothing on screen says that address IS their router, so a privacy-conscious user - exactly the audience this app is built for - sees an unexplained IP in the one feature that admits to sending traffic, and has to go look it up. That address also happens to be an unusual gateway (.147, not .1 - looks like a managed/hotspot network), which makes it read even less like a router.

Fix direction: name the thing, do not just print the address. Something like 'to your router (10.128.67.147)' when the destination is still the auto-detected gateway, falling back to a plain 'to <address>' once the user has edited it to something else - the distinction matters, because after an edit Vanish can no longer claim to know what the address is. Consider also stating it stays on the local network. The existing tile tooltip already explains the one-packet-on-tap contract; it does not explain WHAT is being pinged.

Acceptance: with an auto-detected gateway, the tile identifies the destination as the user's router; after the user edits the destination, it does not claim to know what the address is.
acceptance_criteria: Tile names the auto-detected destination as the user's own router rather than showing a bare IP; a user-edited destination is not described as a router; covered by a UI-interaction assertion.
close_reason:
eex: ambient orbs and the body::before wash are now static, and the prefers-reduced-motion block covers .orb/.pulse (it previously stopped body::before and nothing else, so a user asking their OS for less motion still got three animating layers). Functional indicators - the loading spinner and the indeterminate wait bar - are deliberately left animating: freezing a progress indicator does not read as less motion, it reads as a hung app. Dead @keyframes float removed. Measured after the change with the same harness that found it: 0.00% mean, 0.00% peak, 40 samples, zero nonzero samples (was ~30% continuous). The comment on body::before carries the measurement and the two falsified hypotheses so nobody re-adds an always-on animation without reading why it stopped.

kct: the ping tile and the one-time consent dialog now say 'your router (192.168.1.1)' instead of a bare IP, and only while the destination IS the detected gateway - editing it to anything else drops the claim, and retyping the gateway earns it back (compared against the live gateway, not latched off on first edit). 5 new assertions in the Audit-Mode UI suite drive the real DOM through detected -> edited -> restored.

npm test 442/0 (was 437/0).

title: Bulk queue: platform-wrapped games (Steam, Epic) need custom 'needs attention' feedback, not the generic silent-switch retry message
description:
Operator, live bulk-queue use 2026-08-11 (screenshot: PEAK marked NEEDS ATTENTION, 'The uninstaller did not finish on its own', Retry button offered). PEAK is a Steam game - its registry UninstallString is Steam's own launcher (typically "...\steam.exe" steam://uninstall/<appid>), not a native per-app uninstaller. The generic Rule 15 heuristic (/qn, /S, --silent, -quiet) and the Retry button are both meaningless here: retrying the same silent switches against steam.exe will never work, because Steam intentionally requires its own client UI (or the steam:// URI, which still needs Steam running and interactive) to confirm a game removal - there is no vendor silent-uninstall switch to guess at.

Operator: 'peak uninstalled through steam, so we need custom feedback for apps like platform wrapped games like steam games.'
design:
DETECTION: match the resolved UninstallString/executable against known platform-launcher signatures before falling into the generic heuristic path. Confirmed signatures to start from (steam.exe is the concrete one seen live; scanner.ps1 already reads Steam's own registry key at HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Valve\Steam / HKCU:\Software\Valve\Steam for the library-size backfill, Get-SteamLibrarySizes - same install path can confirm a match):
- Steam: UninstallString contains 'steam.exe' or matches 'steam://uninstall/'.
- Epic Games: UninstallString/executable references EpicGamesLauncher.exe or 'com.epicgames.launcher://uninstall'.
- Likely worth the same treatment later: GOG Galaxy, Battle.net, Ubisoft Connect, EA app - not confirmed live yet, lower priority than Steam/Epic.

UX: when a queue item's uninstall string matches one of these, do not offer the generic 'Retry' (retrying identical silent switches cannot succeed) or the generic 'uninstaller did not finish on its own' text. Instead: name the platform explicitly ('This is a Steam game - Steam manages its own uninstalls') and tell the user the one thing that actually works (open Steam, Library, right-click the game, Uninstall) OR, if acceptable scope, have Vanish launch the platform's own uninstall URI/flow directly (steam://uninstall/<appid> can be opened via ShellExecute, which hands off to the running Steam client - needs Steam to already be running, and does still show Steam's own confirmation UI, so it is not a silent path either, just the CORRECT non-silent path instead of a doomed silent one). Recommend starting with the explanatory-message version (no new engine capability, matches this project's default of not inventing automation without a clear source) and only add the direct steam:// handoff as a deliberate follow-up if the message alone is not enough.
close_reason:
Shipped. lib/platforms.js detects the six storefront launchers (Steam, Epic, GOG Galaxy, Battle.net, Ubisoft Connect, EA app) from a program's UninstallString. When one matches, the bulk queue stops saying 'the uninstaller did not finish on its own' - which was false, there was no uninstaller to finish - and instead names the platform, says why Vanish stopped, and gives the route that works. The Retry button is WITHHELD, because retry re-runs the identical command and against a launcher that is the same doomed request with a second button press.

Deliberately not implemented, per the issue's own recommendation: launching steam://uninstall/ ourselves. It still needs Steam running and still shows Steam's confirmation UI, so it automates nothing the user is not already doing while adding a URI-handler path and implying Vanish drove the removal.

Detection is conservative by design and tested that way: 'C:\Games\SteamlessTool\unins000.exe' and 'C:\Program Files\Steamy Software\uninst.exe' are NOT Steam - the exe is matched as a path component. Suppressing Retry on a program that could have retried successfully is its own wrong answer.

Shared, not duplicated: lib/platforms.js is dual-mode (CommonJS for the main process, classic script for the page) so one set of patterns and one test suite serve both. A second copy in renderer.js is exactly how two code paths drift into disagreeing about what a Steam game is.

Verified: npm test 530/0 (was 501/0), 29 new assertions including the verbatim UninstallString shape from the operator's live report.

title: Diagnostic: detect and surface an elevation attempt that reports success but lands in Audit Mode
description: Operator pushback 2026-08-10 on the 69a sandbox investigation: my conclusion that the observed elevate-relaunch loop was a Windows Sandbox UAC environment issue rested on one PowerShell test, not proof against an app-side bug. Rather than keep speculating, added instrumentation so the NEXT occurrence produces concrete evidence: a one-shot marker written just before quitting on attemptElevatedRelaunch's success path, read and always deleted on the very next boot. If that next boot is NOT elevated, it is definitive proof Vanish's own relaunch reported success while the actual result was not elevated - logged to the oplog and surfaced to the user as an explicit toast (not a silent loop) on the very next launch, naming whether UAC appears disabled on the machine as a likely explanation.
close_reason:
Implemented: store.elevationAttemptPath() (a JSON marker in the state directory), written by attemptElevatedRelaunch right after Start-Process reports success (main.js), read and ALWAYS deleted on the very next boot's bootstrap sequence regardless of outcome (so a stale marker from a crash or a machine sleeping mid-relaunch can never misfire on a later, unrelated launch). A marker only counts as evidence of the CURRENT boot if it is both present and recent (under 5 minutes old, and not from the future - clock skew guard); if this boot came back non-elevated under those conditions, it is logged to the oplog as relaunch-elevated-mismatch with the full Get-UacDiagnostics snapshot, and surfaced once (get-tier's elevationMismatch field is read-then-cleared, so it shows exactly once, not on every poll) as an explicit toast naming whether UAC appears disabled as a likely cause.

This directly answers the operator's correction: it stops relying on inference from black-box symptoms (app closes, reopens, still shows Audit Mode) and instead gives a definitive yes/no the next time it happens - was this a genuinely-non-elevated relaunch, logged and shown, or (if the diagnostic stays silent on a repeat of the loop) evidence the app never even attempted Start-Process at all, which would point somewhere else entirely.

Verified against the REAL main.js boot sequence (not a mock) in a headless-harness electron process, since this genuinely needed real file I/O and the real bootstrap timing: (1) a marker written ~1s before boot IS detected, logged, returned once via get-tier, and confirmed NOT returned on a second get-tier call in the same session (one-shot); (2) a 10-minutes-stale marker is correctly ignored (no mismatch reported) but still deleted; (3) the marker file is deleted in both cases, proving it can never accumulate or misfire later. Also verified the renderer's toast wiring renders the exact expected text, including the UAC-disabled-likely-cause note, via an offscreen harness.

One real methodology mistake caught while verifying, worth recording: the first version of this test ran without VANISH_HEADLESS_HARNESS=1, so main.js's own createWindow() fired as normal, and the REAL renderer's own checkElevation()/getTier() call consumed the one-shot diagnostic before my own explicit test invocation ever read it - the test reported 'not working' when the code was actually correct, a false negative from testing without accounting for a side effect (window creation) the code under test was never responsible for. npm test 404/0.

title: Startup elevation toggle: no in-app way back to Audit Mode from an already-elevated session
description: Operator, live sandbox testing 2026-08-10 (kt0): 'it starts in admin mode as expected, but there is no way to return to audit mode.' Turning off 'Always start with administrator rights' only ever changed what the NEXT independent launch does - flipping it while already elevated had no effect on the current session, and there was no in-app path back to Audit Mode except fully closing the app and finding the exe again unelevated.
notes: LIVE TEST 2026-08-10, v2 (runas /trustlevel:0x20000): CONFIRMED PASS by the operator. Toggle off while elevated, Restart now clicked, no UAC prompt (correct, none expected on this direction), app closed and reopened genuinely in Audit Mode this time - the v1 Shell.Application COM approach's failure (recorded above) is fixed. Full round trip (elevate up via kt0's toggle + real UAC prompt, then de-elevate down via this button) confirmed working end to end.
close_reason:
Added a symmetric 'Restart now' button next to the toggle in Settings > Startup, shown only when the toggle's new target disagrees with the currently-running tier (updateStartupRestartButton, keyed off isAdmin vs the toggle's checked state) - hidden once they agree, so it never suggests a restart that would do nothing. Clicking it applies whichever direction is needed to THIS session instead of only the next independent launch: up reuses the existing relaunchElevated/requestElevation path; down is new (requestDeelevation/relaunch-deelevated).

De-elevation could not reuse relaunch-elevated's Start-Process -Verb RunAs mechanism: a bare child process launched from an elevated parent INHERITS that elevation (Windows only ADDS privilege via UAC, it never drops it on a plain CreateProcess). scanner.ps1's new relaunch-deelevated action routes through Shell.Application COM instead, which asks the desktop's own explorer.exe to start the process - the standard, documented way to get a process at explorer's own (standard user) integrity from an elevated caller. No UAC prompt is possible or expected on this path, by design: UAC governs requesting MORE privilege, not giving it up.

Added a second tiny static splash file (splash-deelevate.html, correct copy for this direction - the elevate one wrongly says Windows is asking permission, which is not true when dropping rights) and registered it in package.json's files list (would otherwise have been silently absent from every packaged build, invisible in npm start - caught by checking, not by a test, since nothing currently asserts the files list against files on disk). Made the shared elevation-wait-overlay's title dynamic (was hardcoded to elevate-specific text) so both directions read correctly.

Verified end to end in an offscreen electron harness at both starting tiers: agreeing state hides the button, a mismatch shows it, and clicking triggers the correct direction's IPC call and overlay copy (confirmed by the exact wording shown, not just that SOME overlay appeared). scanner.ps1 parse-checked clean (Parser]::ParseFile, no execution). Full de-elevation could not be tested end-to-end from this unelevated shell without spawning a visible process on the host, which was deliberately avoided - needs a real elevated session, which the operator was already mid-testing in the Windows Sandbox when this was found. npm test 404/0, icon set 57/57 (no new icons needed, fa-rotate-right already existed).

title: All Programs: multi-select rows and 'Add N to queue' (the real fix for a bulk feature)
description:
Split out of 2pc 2026-08-09. Building a bulk queue today is N x (click row -> details sidebar opens -> click 'Add to bulk queue'), verified: there are 0 checkboxes in #apps-tbody. For a feature literally named 'Bulk uninstall queue' that is the core friction, and it is the one thing the three cheap 2pc fixes did not address.

Scope: a checkbox column in the All Programs table, a header select-all that respects the ACTIVE FILTER (not the whole list), a persistent 'Add N to queue' action, and shift-click range selection. Must respect the same guards the single-item path uses - guardFullMode and guardProtected are currently applied in the btn-queue-app handler (renderer.js:1160), so a bulk add has to apply them per item and report which were skipped and why, rather than silently dropping protected entries.

Pairs with 5b0: filter to a publisher or type, select all, queue - that combination is what makes both features worth more than either alone. Worth deciding 5b0's column-filter scope first so the select-all semantics are defined against real filter state.
close_reason:
Shipped. Checkbox column + shift-click range select + select-all (rendered/filtered rows only, pruned on re-filter) + persistent 'Add N to queue'. Guards shared with the single-item path via a new appProtectionBlock classifier, so protected/feature entries are refused BY NAME in one summary toast and never reach queueAdd. Selection keyed by app.id so it survives a re-sort; the shift anchor is dropped by one, being positional.

Three defects found while wiring, all fixed: (1) ri6's nowrap rule is positional (nth-child 3/4) and the new leading column had silently shifted it onto Type/Date, letting Size wrap again - moved to 4/5; (2) the selection caption and filter caption share one slot, so a live selection hid the filter status entirely, re-creating the 2026-08-05 'a filter that says nothing about itself' bug - the selection caption now carries that sentence, with a regression assertion; (3) queueAddSelected resolved ids against allApps only, so a selected Windows optional feature would have disappeared from both the added count and the skipped list.

Verified: npm test 437/0 (was 404/0). 33 new assertions in the Full Mode UI suite driving the real DOM - checkbox clicks, a synthetic shift-click, a re-sort, a filter, select-all, and a bulk add with a protected and a feature row mixed in, asserting queueAdd was called exactly 3 times for 5 selected. Plus an offscreen screenshot confirming column geometry, indeterminate header state and the live caption. Packaged build: dist/win-unpacked/resources/app.asar extracted and diffed - renderer.js/index.html/index.css/main.js/preload.js IDENTICAL to source; scanner.ps1 and corrections.json sha256 IDENTICAL (renderer-only change, as expected). NSIS installer rebuilt 19:49; the portable target could not be rebuilt - dist/Vanish-0.3.0-portable.exe is locked by a running Vanish-0.3.0-portable.exe (PID 27764), operator closing it.

title: UI interaction suites never open the Health Advisor tab - a whole tab was broken under test and nothing failed
description:
Found 2026-08-09 while implementing hks. renderer.js called five window.api methods that test/fixtures/stub-preload.js did not define at all (getNetworkActivity, networkHoldState/Apply/Revert, startupAction). Opening the Health Advisor tab under the fixture therefore rendered nothing but 'Could not read your system information: window.api.getNetworkActivity is not a function' - and npm test still reported 371/0, because neither test/ui-interaction-verify.js nor test/ui-interaction-full-verify.js ever navigates to that tab. The fixture gap is now fixed (all 48 window.api methods covered, verified by diff), but the COVERAGE hole that let it hide is not: a tab can be completely dead and the suite stays green.

Scope: add Health Advisor coverage to the UI interaction suite - navigate to the tab, assert the System Overview cards, Storage, Network Activity verdict and Startup Items sections each render without an error state, and hit-test the controls (Refresh, Measure again, Hold). Consider a cheap generic guard too: after visiting each tab, assert no .panel-state.error is present anywhere, which would have caught this class of failure on any tab.
close_reason: Added a generic per-tab render guard to test/ui-interaction-verify.js: it now actually CLICKS each of the 8 tabs (the pre-existing loop only hit-tested that the nav item was clickable, which is why a completely dead tab stayed invisible to the suite), then asserts a panel is visible, that it contains no VISIBLE .panel-state.error, and that no 'is not a function' text reached it. Kept generic rather than per-tab content assertions, because the failure being guarded against - 'this whole panel blew up' - looks identical on every tab and a generic check keeps working as panels gain content. Two things found while writing it: (1) a false positive of my own - #vault-error on the Quarantine panel is a permanently-present placeholder hidden by inline style, so the check now filters on offsetParent !== null rather than needing to know which panels carry one; (2) proof the guard actually works - temporarily renaming getNetworkActivity out of the fixture reproduced the original failure and the suite went red on the audit tab, and notably it was the 'is not a function' assertion that caught it, not the .panel-state.error one (that panel renders its error with different markup), so both assertions earn their place. Suite went 62 -> 86; npm test 371 -> 395 passed, 0 failed.

title: Network Activity: high connection count on one program reads as alarming with no context - add reassuring per-type explanation
description:
Operator, 2026-08-09, after the h8j verdict fix: '15 programs with open connections is unremarkable - sure, but one program holding 54 open connections looks worrisome. perhaps a reassuring tooltip explaining normal behaviour for an app of that type would be helpful?'

The Connections open column is a bare integer. A browser, a sync client (OneDrive/Dropbox), a game launcher (Steam/Epic), an antivirus, or a P2P-ish updater (Delivery Optimization) all legitimately hold dozens of sockets; a text editor holding 54 would be odd. Without that framing the number reads as a threat indicator, which is exactly the security/firewall framing Rule 6 says this panel must NOT drift toward - so the answer is context, not a risk score.

Scope: a per-row explanation (tooltip or expandable note) that says what is normal for THAT KIND of program, driven by a small local classification of the process name (browser / sync / launcher / security / updater / system / other). Must not claim a verdict about safety, must not imply Vanish is judging the process, and must not require any network I/O or reverse-DNS (INV-4). Explicitly reassurance + context, not detection.
close_reason: Added a local process-name classifier (NET_PROGRAM_KINDS, renderer.js) covering browsers, file-sync clients, game launchers, chat/meeting apps, security software, updaters/delivery services, developer tools, media apps and Windows components, each with a plain-language sentence on why that KIND of program legitimately holds many sockets. Every connection-count cell gets a title with the count restated as 'a count of connections, not bandwidth', plus the per-kind explanation; counts >= 10 for a recognised program also get a VISIBLE muted note ('normal for a web browser') in the row, because the complaint was that the bare number alarms on sight and a hover-only tooltip does not fix that. Unrecognised programs get text that explicitly says a missing description means nothing either way, so 'not in the list' can never read as 'suspicious'. Deliberately no risk score, no safe/unsafe verdict and no trusted-process list - that is the security/firewall framing Rule 6 keeps this panel out of. Entirely local string matching: no lookup, no reverse-DNS, no outbound I/O (INV-4). Verified against the operator's own case (chrome/54 -> 'normal for a web browser') plus steam/18, avp/12, an unrecognised app at 31 and notepad at 2, in an offscreen electron harness. npm test 371/0.

title: All Programs table: column 2 header says 'Publisher' but renders a Desktop/Windows App/Feature type badge
description: Found while fixing ri6 (sidebar column-compression). index.html's all-apps-table thead labels column 2 'Publisher' (line 224), but renderTable() in renderer.js (~line 744) actually fills that td with a badge-type span (Desktop/Windows App/Feature) - the real publisher text is nested inside column 1 under the app name (.app-publisher-name). Only one place in index.html says 'Publisher' and it is this stale header. Fix: rename the header to 'Type' to match what the column actually shows.
close_reason: Renamed the All Programs table's column 2 header from 'Publisher' to 'Type' to match what renderTable() actually puts there (a Desktop/Windows App/Feature badge) - the real publisher text lives under the app name in column 1 and always has. No test asserted the old header text. npm test 371/0.

title: Sticky table headers across all scrollable views
description: Operator: all column names across all views need to show persistently, regardless of scrolling. Currently table headers (All Programs, Task Manager, Network Activity process table, System Clean findings, Force Uninstall results) scroll away with the body. Needs position: sticky; top: 0 (with an opaque background matching each tables row background, since the app already relies on translucent glass panels elsewhere) applied consistently - touches multiple table instances, not a single CSS rule.
close_reason: Applied position:sticky;top:0 (near-opaque + blur background matching the app's existing glass-panel look, e.g. .wizard-modal) to .apps-table th, one shared class used by all 4 actual column-header tables in the app: All Programs, Health Advisor's startup table, Task Manager, and Network Activity's process table - confirmed by grep there are no other <table><thead> instances. System Clean findings and Force Uninstall results were in the operator's original list but turned out to be div-based expandable item rows with no column-header row at all (verified in renderer.js renderCleanerBody/renderForceResults) - nothing there to make sticky, scope narrowed accordingly. Verified the mechanism with getBoundingClientRect across 6 scroll positions in an offscreen electron harness: the header settles into its stuck position within the first ~100px of scroll (an 8px one-time shift from the table's own border-spacing, imperceptible) and then holds pixel-identical through scrollTop 100/300/400/700/900. npm test 371/0.

title: Task Manager: GPU per-row gaps confusing (slow 15s sample vs fast list refresh), and the summed-engine percent needs an in-UI explanation
description: Operator: vanish seems to be consuming 30% of gpu but i still dont see the gpu indicators, and asked to explain the 30% figure. Two separate things: (1) GPU% is only sampled every 15s (GPU_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_MS, renderer.js) while the process list itself refreshes every 1-60s (configurable) - a process whose PID is new since the last GPU sample shows - not because it has no GPU usage but because no sample has covered it yet; this gap reads as missing/broken to a user with no framing. (2) The per-process percent is a SUM across that process engines (3D, copy, video decode, etc, capped at 100) per Get-GpuUsageByProcess own code comment - not a claim of exact parity with real Task Managers internal weighting. Neither of these is explained anywhere in the UI, only in code comments - needs a visible explanation (tooltip, help icon, or inline note) so the number is not read as either broken or as gospel.
close_reason: Two fixes, both in-UI where a user can actually read them. (1) Per-row gaps: scanner.ps1's Get-GpuUsageByProcess drops any engine reading of 0 ('if ($sample.CookedValue -le 0) { continue }'), so a PID absent from byPid was ambiguous - 'measured, idle' and 'never measured, process is newer than the sample' both rendered as the same bare '-'. Now captures the PID set at sample time (BEFORE the await, since the counter read happens at call start, not 1.5-3s later when it returns) and renders three distinct states: 'measuring...' before the first sample of the session completes, an honest '0%' when the process WAS covered by the sample and simply had no GPU work, and '-' only for a process genuinely newer than the last sample - each with its own explanatory title. (2) Summed-engine semantics: added a visible .panel-inline-note under the Task Manager header plus a title on the GPU column header, both stating the 15s cadence and that the percentage sums a process's work across the GPU's engines (3D/video/copy) so it will not always match Task Manager's own figure - previously only a code comment. Also fixed a shared-fixture gap found on the way (AGP-5 recurrence): getGpuUsage/getGpuVendors were missing from test/fixtures/stub-preload.js entirely even though opening the Task Manager tab calls both - added at the fixture level, not worked around locally. Verified all four cell states in an offscreen electron harness. npm test 371/0.

title: Network Activity: ping reiterated (manual-tap only) - still conflicts with the zero-network-I/O test invariant, needs an explicit decision
description: Operator asked again for ping (this time explicitly manual/on-demand, not continuous background) after the prior sessions explanation of INV-4 (test/network-verify.ps1 greps the whole engine for Test-Connection/Test-NetConnection/etc and fails the build if either appears, regardless of how often it would be called). A manual-tap ping is still an outbound network probe from the engine - the test does not distinguish frequency, only presence of the capability. This needs an explicit decision, not a silent implementation either way: accepting it means updating the zero-network-I/O test itself, the About page's Network use while running: None claim, and probably a one-time on-tap warning; declining it again means re-explaining why more convincingly or finding a proxy metric that does not require an actual probe (e.g. TCP connect-time to the already-known default gateway, which is arguably narrower but still real network I/O).
design:
RECOMMENDATION: ACCEPT, tightly scoped. Reasoning, and the honest cost.

The invariant's real promise is 'nothing about you or your PC leaves this machine'. That promise stays 100% intact under a manual ping: an ICMP echo carries no data about the user, and the destination already sees every packet they send. What breaks is the IMPLEMENTATION of that promise - 'zero network calls, grep-checkable' - which is a stronger, cheaper-to-verify claim than the promise itself.

What is actually being traded: today the guarantee is machine-checkable by anyone in one grep, with no code reading and no trust in the maintainer. After an exception it becomes 'no network calls except the one behind an explicit user tap', which cannot be verified by grep - only by reading the call graph. For a tool whose entire pitch is auditability that is a real loss, and it is the operator's call whether the feature is worth it, which is why this stayed a decision.

If ACCEPTED, all five of these are required, not optional:
1. Manual tap only. No timer, no auto-run on panel open, no run-on-refresh.
2. Rewrite network-verify.ps1's INV-4 section rather than deleting it: keep the blanket ban on the other five strings, and replace the two named ping assertions with a scoped pair - assert Test-Connection appears exactly once in scanner.ps1, inside the named ping action and nowhere else. A weaker invariant that is still enforced beats an invariant that was deleted.
3. Reword the About card to separate the permanent promise from the mechanism: 'Vanish never sends anything about you or your PC anywhere' (absolute) + 'It makes no network connections at all unless you tap Ping, which sends a single echo request and nothing else' (precise).
4. One-time explanatory confirmation on first tap, then remembered - naming what is sent, to where, and that it is the only outbound traffic the app can make.
5. User-visible destination, defaulted to the default gateway and editable. Never a hardcoded third-party IP - 1.1.1.1/8.8.8.8 silently tells Cloudflare/Google the user is running this tool.

If DECLINED: kp0 should be closed as wont-fix rather than left open a third time, with the About card's absolute claim recorded as the reason - so the next session does not reopen the same debate. anc has already shipped without it and the tile grid takes a fourth tile with no rework if this later flips.
notes:
EXACT CONSTRAINT, verified 2026-08-09. test/network-verify.ps1:46-58 greps scanner.ps1 as raw text for seven strings: Invoke-WebRequest, Invoke-RestMethod, System.Net.WebClient, Net.Sockets.TcpClient, Test-NetConnection, Test-Connection, System.Net.NetworkInformation.Ping. Test-NetConnection and Test-Connection additionally get their own named assertions, with a comment stating the intent explicitly: 'Naming them individually means the next person adding one has to delete an assertion to do it.' That is a deliberate speed bump aimed at exactly this request.

About page claim it backs (index.html, 'Nothing leaves this PC' card): 'Vanish makes no network connections while it runs. No tracking, no cloud lookups, no update checks. Even the icons and fonts come from this PC, so nothing is downloaded.'

There is NO local proxy for latency. Ping measures round-trip time to a remote host; nothing in adapter byte counters, DO/BITS state or connection tables approximates it. The 'TCP connect to the default gateway' idea floated earlier is still real outbound I/O and additionally measures the LAN hop, not the internet - it would produce a reassuring ~1ms number that answers a different question than the one a user asking for ping is asking.
close_reason: ACCEPTED and implemented, all five non-negotiable conditions from the recommendation shipped: (1) manual tap only - Invoke-NetworkPing/runPing have no timer, no interval, no auto-call anywhere, the click handler is the only caller; (2) test/network-verify.ps1's INV-4 rewritten not deleted - the other 6 network-call strings stay an absolute ban, Test-NetConnection stays fully banned, and Test-Connection is now asserted to appear exactly once IN CODE (comment-aware counting, since the file's own kp0 prose mentions the string) and specifically inside Invoke-NetworkPing, nowhere else - 39/0 including 7 new assertions; (3) About page reworded to separate the absolute promise ('nothing about you or this PC ever leaves it') from the mechanism (the Ping tile, named explicitly), plus the facts-table 'Network use while running' row which the design doc flagged and a grep found was NOT 'None' any more; (4) one-time confirmDialog before the first-ever tap naming the destination and stating it is the only outbound traffic the app sends, gated on a new pingConsentGiven setting - declining does not set it, so the next tap asks again; (5) destination defaults to the adapter's own gatewayAddress (new field, threaded through Get-NetAdapterSnapshot -> Get-NetworkActivity), is user-visible in the tile and editable via a pencil icon, never a hardcoded third-party IP. Fourth rate tile added to anc's grid as anticipated. Verified end to end in an offscreen electron harness: default destination populated from a real gateway, consent dialog appears and mentions the destination, ping runs and shows '12 ms', second tap skips the dialog (remembered), destination edit updates and persists, screenshot captured. Also verified for real: powershell test/network-verify.ps1 including live loopback (127.0.0.1, always answers) and TEST-NET-1 (192.0.2.1, RFC 5737 reserved/unreachable, cannot accidentally probe a real host) round trips. Fixed the same class of fixture gap on the way (networkPing was missing from stub-preload.js). npm test 395 -> 404/0, icon set 55 -> 57/57 (added fa-tower-broadcast, fa-pen).

title: Bulk uninstall queue flow feels invasive, causes friction for its own interactions
description: Operator feedback (screenshot of the Bulk uninstall queue bar): the flow is invasive and causes friction for its own interactions - vague as reported, needs a first pass in the next session to concretize what specifically is friction-causing (the queue bar taking permanent screen space? the confirm-dialog chain? something else) before redesigning. Start by walking the actual queue-add -> queue-start -> per-item-progress flow end to end and noting every point that feels heavier than it needs to be.
design:
RECOMMENDATION - three cheap fixes first, then decide on the big one.

CHEAP (do these regardless, they address 2/3/5 directly):
a. Stop auto-expanding on add. Expand on the FIRST add only, then respect the user's collapsed state - one flag.
b. Make the close button actually dismiss (hide the panel, keep the queue). Re-open from a persistent count chip in the header, so the queue is never lost, just out of the way.
c. Toast only on the first add, then update the panel's own count badge silently. The badge already exists and is the better feedback channel.

BIGGER, needs an operator call:
d. Multi-select in All Programs (checkbox column + 'Add N to queue'). This is the real fix for a bulk feature and would also make 5b0's column-filter work more valuable - filter to a publisher, select all, queue. Notably it does NOT need the queue panel redesigned.
e. Only if a-d are not enough: move the queue from a floating panel to its own tab or a docked bottom strip. Recommend deferring this - a-d remove most of the friction at a fraction of the cost, and a floating panel that behaves itself is genuinely useful for watching progress while working in another tab.

Suggest doing a-c now as one small change, then re-showing it to the operator before committing to d or e.
notes:
FLOW WALKED 2026-08-09, measured at the app's own default window size (1080x720, main.js createWindow). The report was vague; these are the five concrete mechanisms behind it.

1. THE PANEL COVERS THE APP LIST, ON EVERY TAB. .queue-panel is position:fixed right:22 bottom:22, width 400px, max-height 62vh, z-index 60 (index.css:2613). Measured with 6 pending items: it occupies 366 x 393 px of the .apps-list-container - 37% of viewport width and 58% of its height. renderQueue() adds .active purely on items.length > 0 (renderer.js:3688) and nothing ties it to a tab, so it also floats over Task Manager, System Clean, Quarantine, Settings and About for as long as anything is queued.

2. IT RE-EXPANDS ITSELF EVERY TIME YOU ADD. queueAddApp() calls classList.remove('collapsed') on every add (renderer.js:3617). Collapsing it is therefore undone by the next add - queueing 6 apps means collapsing it 6 times. This is most precisely the operator's 'causes friction for its own interactions'.

3. THE CLOSE BUTTON DOES NOT CLOSE. btn-queue-close only toggles .collapsed; there is no way to dismiss the panel while the queue has items.

4. NO MULTI-SELECT, IN A BULK FEATURE. Verified 0 checkboxes in #apps-tbody. Building a queue of N apps is N x (click row -> sidebar opens -> click Add to bulk queue), and the sidebar that holds the Add button is itself in the bottom-right region the queue panel competes with.

5. A TOAST PER ADD. queueAddApp() fires a success toast on every single add, so the same 6-app queue produces 6 transient notifications on top of everything above.

MEASUREMENT ARTIFACT, recorded so it is not mistaken for a finding: an attempt to measure queue-vs-sidebar overlap returned width 0 for the sidebar. That was my own script adding .active and reading getBoundingClientRect in the same tick, before the 0.3s width transition (added in ri6) had run - not a product bug. The table overlap figures above are unaffected because the table does not animate.
close_reason:
Walked the real add -> start -> progress flow and measured it (findings recorded in this issue's notes: the panel covers 366x393px of the app list on EVERY tab, re-expands on every add, close only collapses, no multi-select in a bulk feature, one toast per add). Shipped the three cheap fixes from the recommendation:

(a) The panel now announces itself ONCE, when the queue goes from empty to non-empty, instead of calling classList.remove('collapsed') on every add - so deliberately collapsing it is no longer undone by the next add. Emptying the queue resets the announcement so the next batch opens for the user again.
(b) Toast only on that first add, with wording that tells the user what to do next ('Add more, then press Start'); adds 2..N update the header count badge silently, which is visible even when collapsed.
(c) Collapsed panel shrinks to its own header: measured 400x419 -> 391x57, about 87% less screen area. Honest limit noted in the CSS - the width barely moves because the header's own controls need ~391px; the height is the win.

Verified in an offscreen electron harness at the app's real default size (1080x720) via the fixture's own queueResponse mechanism: first add expands and shows count 1, a user-collapsed panel stays collapsed through adds 2 and 3 while the badge goes to 3, and emptying the queue resets the flag. npm test 395/0.

NOT done, left as follow-ups needing an operator call rather than silently deciding: multi-select in All Programs (filed as the natural fix for a bulk feature, and it pairs with 5b0), and moving the queue out of a floating panel entirely - recommended against for now, since a-c remove most of the friction and a well-behaved floating panel is genuinely useful for watching progress from another tab.

title: All Programs: details/uninstall sidebar is fixed-width, blank until first selection, causes cut-off rows on default window size
description: Operator: clicking an app item should compress the row list to make room for the uninstall sidebar - sidebar width is hardcoded, which cuts off table rows when the app opens at its smaller default window size. Also: until the first program is selected, that sidebar space sits blank/unused rather than showing anything useful (a hint, a summary, or collapsing entirely). Two related but distinct fixes: (1) responsive layout so the sidebar does not clip the table at default window width, (2) a non-blank default/empty state for the sidebar before any selection.
close_reason: Two distinct fixes. (1) The sidebar's flexbox compression of the app list was already correct (.apps-list-container is flex:1) - the actual defect was Date/Size, short fixed-format columns, having no width floor and wrapping to two lines ('2026-' / '01-01') once compressed, reading as broken. Scoped nowrap to just those two columns (#all-apps-table th/td :nth-child(3/4)) so table-layout:auto reserves their min-content width and Name/Publisher (which already wrap cleanly) absorb the squeeze instead. (2) The panel claimed its full clamp(250px,28%,340px) width from the workspace even while invisible (opacity:0) before any selection - added #details-sidebar:not(.active) { width:0; padding:0; border-width:0 } so the app list gets full width by default and the panel expands only on selection. Scoped to the All Programs sidebar specifically; Task Manager's process-details panel is untouched. Verified via geometry checks (no-selection: list gets 752 of 840px workspace width vs. previously losing 250-340px permanently; selected: Date/Size stay single-line nowrap, table does not overflow its container) and two captured screenshots in an offscreen electron harness. npm test 371/0.

title: Should Vanish silently automate/direct existing third-party uninstallers via switches?
description: Operator question, needs a product decision, not a silent implementation: can/should Vanish run an ALREADY-INSTALLED programs own uninstaller silently (passing known silent switches), rather than launching its interactive UI? corrections.json + the Rule 15 switch resolver already do some of this for Vanishs own uninstall queue - clarify current scope (which flows already do this, which dont) and decide whether to extend it, and to what surfaces (single-item Clean Uninstall vs bulk queue vs both).
design:
RECOMMENDATION (needs operator sign-off, all three are product calls not engineering ones):

1. USER CHOICE - recommend YES, add it. Right now silent is forced with no way to opt out. Some users legitimately want the vendor uninstaller's own UI (it sometimes offers 'keep my settings', or a reason-for-leaving step that unlocks a refund/licence release). Suggest a per-uninstall choice, defaulting to silent, remembered in settings. Low cost: the resolver already returns both baseArgs and arguments, so 'interactive' is just passing baseArgs alone.

2. TELL THE USER WHICH METHOD WAS USED - recommend YES. resolved.method is already 'corrections' or 'heuristic' and already logged, but never shown. A heuristic guess is materially less certain than a verified corrections.json entry, and the completion screen currently presents both identically. Same honesty principle as xw2/h8j.

3. GROW corrections.json - recommend YES but slowly, and only with a cited vendor source per entry, matching the existing meta.verified discipline. Explicitly do NOT bulk-import a community switch list: a wrong silentArgs value is worse than no entry, because the heuristic fallback at least degrades to showing the UI rather than passing a switch that means something else to that specific installer.

NOT recommended: making the heuristic more aggressive by trying candidates in sequence until one 'works'. There is no reliable success signal to iterate on, and a wrong switch passed to an arbitrary vendor uninstaller is not guaranteed to be a no-op.
notes:
SCOPE QUESTION RESOLVED 2026-08-09 by reading the code. The premise 'should Vanish do this' is already answered: it DOES, on both surfaces, via the same resolver.

Single-item Clean Uninstall: main.js uninstall-native Step 3 calls resolve-uninstall-args (main.js:539) then run-uninstaller with the resolved switches.
Bulk queue: lib/queue.js:269 calls the identical resolve-uninstall-args.

Resolver (scanner.ps1 Resolve-UninstallArgs:3781): step 1 matches corrections.json (11 apps: Chrome, Firefox, Slack, Zoom, Steam etc; longest displayName substring wins, publisher narrows ambiguity, silentArgs REPLACES registry args, executable kept). Step 2 falls back to the Rule 15 heuristic sequence /qn -> /S -> --silent -> -quiet, with /qn dropped for anything not detected as MSI.

Engine also already detects when an uninstaller shows its UI anyway: Invoke-Uninstaller polls MainWindowHandle and returns interactive=true, which main.js records in the oplog.

So there is no missing capability. The three REAL remaining questions are below.
close_reason:
All three recommended items shipped.

1. USER CHOICE: single-item Clean Uninstall's wizard has a new 'Run silently' toggle (screen 3, scr-native-run - placed right next to the button it affects rather than screen 1, see below for why) defaulting from a new preferSilentUninstall setting (default true), remembered whenever changed. Interactive means 'use baseArgs alone, skip the resolved silent switch' - main.js's uninstall-native handler now passes arguments: req.interactive === true ? '' : resolved.arguments, exactly the low-cost change the recommendation anticipated. Bulk queue is deliberately untouched - unattended is the whole point of a queue, so it keeps always-silent-with-interactive-flagged behavior; a per-item choice there would defeat that. Force Uninstall's 'run its own uninstaller' quick path (scanBrokenEntry, no wizard UI) respects the remembered setting as its default instead, via an explicit parameter rather than reading wizard state it has no relationship to.

2. METHOD DISCLOSURE: resolved.method ('corrections' vs 'heuristic') and the interactive-detected flag were already returned by the engine and already logged to the oplog - just never shown. The completion toast now says which switch class was used, and explicitly flags heuristic guesses as unverified for that specific program (matching xw2/h8j's honesty principle: presenting a verified switch and a guessed one identically was the actual problem). Also notes when a silently-requested uninstaller opened its own window anyway.

3. corrections.json growth: no code change - it is already a discipline (cited source + meta.verified per entry), not a capability gap. Recorded as a standing practice, not a task.

Caught and fixed a real regression on the way: the toggle was first placed on screen 1 (scr-config) alongside the restore-point toggle, which grew that screen past the wizard modal's fixed height and pushed the scan-mode cards and restore-point toggle out of the immediately-clickable area - caught by the existing test/ui-interaction-full-verify.js hit-test suite (2 failures). Moved to screen 3 instead (arguably the more natural placement anyway, right before the button it affects) rather than force-fitting screen 1 with a scroll workaround, since scrolling on every single uninstall - a core, high-frequency flow - would have been worse UX than the placement bug it was fixing.

Verified end to end in an offscreen electron harness: the interactive flag threads correctly to the IPC request in both toggle states, the prompt text switches correctly, the setting persists across wizard opens, and both toast variants (verified-switch, unverified-switch, unverified-switch-that-opened-anyway) render the exact expected text. npm test 404/0 throughout, including after the layout fix.

title: Guided tour: spotlight walkthrough, first-launch + on-demand from Settings
description: Operator asked to plan a first-time-install tour, runnable on demand from Settings. Implemented (not just planned): a hand-rolled spotlight overlay (no third-party tour library, same zero-dependency approach as assets/icons.css) - 7 steps covering tier/Audit Mode, All Programs, Health Advisor, System Clean, Quarantine, and where to find the tour again. Auto-shows once on first launch (settings.hasSeenTour), replayable any time via a new Take the tour row in Settings. Caught and fixed a real regression before it shipped: the tours full-screen pointer-events:all overlay auto-started during the Full Mode UI-interaction test suite (fresh hasSeenTour defaults false there) and blocked all 30 of that suites clicks - fixed by adding hasSeenTour:true to the test fixtures stub-preload (an already-onboarded user is the correct default for a UI test fixture), not by weakening the tours real blocking behavior. Also added one ambient animation as a concrete example of the broader animation-ideas ask: a very low-opacity, slow-drifting radial-gradient wash behind the glass panels, respecting prefers-reduced-motion, deliberately subtle for a trust-focused audit tool.
close_reason: Implemented and verified: npm test 371/0 (including the Full Mode regression catch+fix), npm run verify 171/0, icon-verify 3/0. Not visually screenshotted (no safe way to launch a real window and confirm pixel layout this session) - positioning logic (spotlight cutout, tooltip left/right/vertical clamping) is implemented per the documented algorithm and exercised by the UI-interaction test suites getBoundingClientRect-based hit tests, but an operator should take the actual tour once on a real launch to confirm it looks right, not just that it does not crash or block clicks.

title: Network Hold: held transfers not attributable to any row in the process or activity list
description: Operator reports that when background transfers are on hold (Delivery Optimization capped plus BITS jobs suspended, bfh.2), nothing in the Network Activity process table or Task Manager indicates which rows correspond to what is actually being held - the function works but is invisible, hard to confirm by looking at the screen. Needs investigation into what the hold-capture record actually contains (BITS job IDs, process names if any) and whether or how that can be cross-referenced against the process list to mark held rows.
close_reason: renderNetworkHold now lists each held BITS jobs displayName (state.record.bitsJobs, already captured by network-hold-capture, only its Count was ever shown) instead of just a number. True PID-level attribution isnt possible - Get-BitsTransfer exposes no owning-process field - so this is the concrete-but-honest version: name the actual transfers, not a guessed process correlation.

title: Redundant software: waive/override workflow with per-item uninstall shortcuts
description: Get-SoftwareRedundancy groups (renderer.js renderRedundancyGroups) are entirely static today - pills with no interactive element at all, confirmed by reading the full render function. Operator wants: a decision workflow per redundancy group offering (a) a button per app that jumps straight to that apps uninstall wizard (same entry point as the main All Apps list), and (b) a waive-this button that persists an override - the group keeps showing (not hidden), but with a visible you-overrode-this notice, and the same decision buttons still available (waiving is not the same as dismissing). No existing persistence pattern for arbitrary per-item user overrides exists anywhere in the app (only whole-settings-object writes via set-settings, and one in-memory-only, never-persisted, per-session flag for the elevation offer) - needs a new small store concept, e.g. a waivers.json file following the same store.js pattern as settings.json/manifest.json.
close_reason: redundancyWaivers array added to settings.json (lib/store.js, reuses existing get-settings/set-settings IPC - no new store file, no new IPC handler). renderRedundancyGroups (renderer.js) now renders a per-app Review-to-uninstall button (jumps to All Apps tab, clears filters, calls the same selectApp() a manual click would, stops short of auto-opening the wizard since the redundancy apps object is a collapsed family summary not necessarily the live registry row) and a per-group Keep-all-of-these/waive toggle. Waived groups keep rendering with an override notice, exactly as specified (waiving is not dismissing). Fixed 3 icon-verify failures caught by test/icon-verify.js (fa-arrow-up-right-from-square, fa-user-check, fa-check were never in the vendored icon set) by swapping to existing glyphs (fa-magnifying-glass, fa-circle-check) rather than authoring new SVGs under time pressure.

title: Network Activity: enumerate peer IPs per process (no ports, no DNS)
description: Get-NetConnectionsByProcess (scanner.ps1:1395) already collects each processs distinct remote peer IPs into a hashtable, keyed by IP - today only the count is surfaced (peerCount). The IP list itself can be exposed cheaply (already collected, zero new network I/O). Two deliberate limits kept, not reversed: (1) no port numbers - the code deliberately strips the port today with a comment citing Rule 6 (zero-network, local-only privacy stance) to avoid drifting toward security framing; (2) no reverse-DNS hostname resolution - that is network I/O, and would violate INV-4 (test/network-verify.ps1 asserts zero outbound calls from the engine, by name, including the two an author reaches for first).
close_reason: scanner.ps1 Get-NetConnectionsByProcess now returns entry.peers.Keys (the IP list, already being collected) instead of discarding it after Count. Renderer renders an expandable per-row peer-IP list (net-peers-toggle/net-peers-list). No port, no DNS - both limits kept exactly as before.

title: Network Activity: surface upload and download speed (already computed, not displayed)
description: Get-NetworkActivity (scanner.ps1:1433) already computes receiveBytesPerSecond and sendBytesPerSecond per adapter (used today only to derive the busy/quiet verdict and one combined bytes-per-second note) - splitting into a displayed upload/download speed is a renderer-only change, no new engine capability, no new network I/O.
