title: UAC diagnostics: distinguish 'UAC disabled, changeable' from 'UAC disabled/locked by domain Group Policy'
description:
Operator, 2026-08-11: 'uac disabled status is visible to vanish, and it should be able to discern vanish being disabled against it being perm locked, as is common in perm locked corporate machines.'

Get-UacDiagnostics (scanner.ps1) already reads EnableLUA and reports enableLua:false when UAC is off, but treats every disabled case identically. On a domain-joined, GPO-managed corporate machine, EnableLUA is very often force-set to 0 (or force-set to 1 and unable to be turned off) by Group Policy and will silently revert on the next policy refresh if a local admin changes it by hand - materially different from a home/personal machine where the SAME registry value was just switched off once and stays that way. The elevate-toggle's own behavior (trigger UAC if enabled, silently elevate if disabled) does not need to change - Start-Process -Verb RunAs already does exactly this correctly, confirmed live this session (kt0). This is purely a DIAGNOSTIC/MESSAGING improvement: telling the user WHY UAC reads as off, and whether they can expect to change it themselves.
design:
No clean single registry flag distinguishes 'set by GPO' from 'set by hand' for classic UAC values - Windows does not tag policy-origin on these keys. Best achievable, honestly-caveated signal (matches Rule 24 - unknown is not zero):
1. Check domain membership: (Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem).PartOfDomain.
2. If domain-joined, test whether the current (already-admin) token can actually WRITE to HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\EnableLUA (a scratch Set-ItemProperty + revert, or Get-Acl against the key checked against the current identity).
3. Domain-joined AND not writable by an admin token -> report a new cause 'uac-disabled-locked' (or similar) distinct from the existing 'uac-disabled'. Domain-joined but writable, or not domain-joined at all -> keep the existing plain 'uac-disabled'.
Explicitly not attempting: reading actual GPO RSOP data (gpresult /nsopping is slow, not scriptable cheaply, and overkill for a UI hint) or claiming certainty this IS GPO-enforced when the heuristic can only really say 'this looks locked down, likely by policy'. Wording in the UI must say 'likely locked by your organization's policy' or similar, never a flat, overconfident claim.
close_reason:
Shipped in 0.5.0. Get-UacDiagnostics now returns partOfDomain, policyWritable and lockLikely; a new 'uac-disabled-locked' cause carries wording that says the setting is LIKELY enforced by organisation policy and points at whoever administers the PC, instead of telling a corporate user to turn UAC back on (which reverts at the next policy refresh).

TWO DELIBERATE CHANGES FROM THE DESIGN AS FILED, both about not overclaiming:

1. The writability probe only runs when the process is ALREADY ELEVATED. The design said to test whether 'the current (already-admin) token' can write EnableLUA, but nothing enforced that. An unelevated process cannot write HKLM under any circumstances, so running the probe from Audit Mode would report 'locked by policy' on every ordinary home machine in the world - confident, plausible, and completely wrong, which is the exact failure mode this issue exists to prevent. Unelevated leaves policyWritable null. Verified live on this machine: partOfDomain false, isElevatedNow false, policyWritable null, lockLikely false - it correctly claims nothing.

2. It writes a SCRATCH value (VanishWriteProbe) and removes it in a finally block, rather than setting and reverting EnableLUA as the design suggested. Same key, same ACL, same answer, but a failure halfway through leaves a stray registry value instead of a machine with UAC switched off. test/uac-lock-verify.js asserts nothing in the engine ever writes EnableLUA.

WORDING IS PART OF THE CONTRACT and is asserted, not just written: the message must say 'likely', must never assert Group Policy did this (Windows does not record policy-origin on these values), must point at the administrator, and must NOT repeat the personal-machine advice. The unmanaged case still says 'turn UAC back on'.

Verified: test/uac-lock-verify.js 19/19, wired into run-all. Full suite 660 passed, 0 failed.

title: Indicators column and general filtering: add Excel-style column filter/category list across views
description: Operator wants the Task Manager Indicators column (and process/app views generally) to support more categories plus an Excel-like filter list - click a column header, get a checklist of the distinct values present, select which to show. This is a real, larger feature (a reusable column-filter UI component), not a one-line fix - scope which columns/views it applies to first (Indicators in Task Manager is the explicit ask; All Programs type/publisher columns are an obvious extension) before building.
design:
SCOPED 2026-08-09 (the issue's own instruction was to scope before building). Not built yet - deliberately, see the sequencing note at the end.

WHERE IT APPLIES. There are exactly four real column-header tables in the app, all sharing the .apps-table class (confirmed by grep - System Clean and Force Uninstall are div-based item lists with no header row, so they are out of scope by construction):
- Task Manager: Indicators (the explicit ask), plus Process name. NOT CPU/GPU/Memory/Disk - those are continuous numeric values where a distinct-value checklist is meaningless; they want a threshold filter, which is a different control and should not be smuggled into this one.
- All Programs: Type (Desktop/Windows App/Feature - only 3 values, high value) and Publisher (long tail, needs search-within-filter).
- Health Advisor startup table: Source and Status - both small closed sets, cheap wins.
- Network Activity process table: not worth it, the list is already capped at the top 6 rows.

RECOMMENDED SHAPE.
- One function, buildColumnFilter(tableEl, columnIndex, { getRows, onChange }), attached to a header via a small funnel icon that only appears on filterable columns. No framework, no new dependency - matches how the rest of this renderer is written.
- Popover lists DISTINCT VALUES PRESENT IN THE CURRENT DATA with a count each, not a hardcoded enum, so it cannot drift out of sync with what the engine actually returns.
- Search-within-filter box appears only when distinct values exceed ~12 (covers Publisher, stays out of the way for Type).
- Select all / none / invert. Active filters shown as removable chips above the table so a filtered view can never be mistaken for an empty one - this app has a documented history of exactly that confusion (7oo epic, the silent-filter bug).
- Filter state per (view, column), held in renderer memory only. NOT persisted to settings: a filter the user forgot they set, restored silently on next launch, is the same class of bug as the silent filter above.
- Interaction with existing search: AND, and the row count caption must state both ('Showing 12 of 158 - filtered by Type, Publisher').

WHAT TO WATCH.
- Indicators is multi-valued per row (a process can carry several chips), so the filter is 'row matches ANY selected indicator', not equality. Getting this wrong silently under-reports, which is the honesty failure mode this project keeps hitting.
- Sticky headers shipped in h0i - the popover must be positioned against the sticky header's live position and needs a z-index above it (th is z-index 2).
- The empty result state must say 'no rows match this filter' with a clear-filters action, never the generic empty-list copy.

SEQUENCING. Build 5rz (multi-select + 'Add N to queue') FIRST, then this. The pair is what creates the real value - filter to a publisher, select all, queue - and 5rz defines what 'select all' must mean against an active filter. Building this one first risks a select-all semantic that 5rz then has to change.
close_reason:
Shipped in 0.6.5. One shared control (renderer/column-filter.js, 8th renderer script) on all three real column-header tables: All Programs (Publisher on the NAME header, since that is the column publishers are rendered in; Type), Task Manager (Process, Indicators), Health Advisor startup (Source, Status). CPU/GPU/Memory/Disk/PID deliberately excluded - a distinct-value checklist is meaningless for a continuous number, and hiding a threshold control behind the same funnel would misrepresent both.

FOUR DECISIONS THAT ARE THE ACTUAL DESIGN, each failing towards showing too much:
1. State is the set of EXCLUDED values, never the selected ones. With live data (a process starts, a program is removed, a new indicator kind ships), selected-set semantics would withhold a value that did not exist when the filter was set. Hiding something new is the failure this app cannot afford.
2. The checklist is built from the view's whole pool, not the surviving rows - an option list that shrinks as you uncheck is a trap with no way back.
3. A multi-valued row survives while ANY of its values is shown. The two-indicator process stays visible when one is hidden and leaves only when both are; equality would under-report exactly the processes carrying the most warnings. Rows with no value get one synthetic None bucket.
4. Nothing persisted. Asserted, not assumed: setSettings call count is 0 after the whole suite.

Also: the checklist offers the words the CELLS show, via appTypeLabel()/startupSourceLabel()/startupStatusLabel() extracted so the cell and the filter cannot drift - Type reads 'Windows App' not 'UWP', Source reads 'Task' not 'TaskScheduler'.

ACCOUNTABILITY, which is most of the work: caption names the columns ('Showing 12 of 158 programs - filtered by Publisher, Type'); removable chips above each table; empty states name the filter that emptied them and offer a way out. Task Manager and the startup table had NO caption row before this - Task Manager re-samples every 2s, so a filtered list read as a quiet machine.

ONE REAL DEFECT FOUND BY THE TESTS: updateBulkSelectUI tested only filterText/filterType, so with only a column filter set the bulk-selection caption dropped the filter sentence - the 2026-08-05 silent-filter bug through a new door. Fixed in queue-clean.js. Found by asserting the RULE, not the two filters that existed when the rule was written. Second find: fa-filter did not exist in the vendored icon set, and an undefined glyph here paints a blank square rather than throwing (icon-verify caught it).

VERIFIED: test/column-filter-verify.js, 81 assertions, registered in run-all.ps1. Full suite 838 passed / 0 failed (was 757). details-panel-layout-verify (52 assertions, several widths) confirms the funnels did not truncate a header or overflow the process table - clippedHeaders empty, container client 620 = scroll 620 at the operator's 1110x741. Offscreen screenshots of All Programs (popover + chip + caption) and Task Manager narrow reviewed.

NOT VERIFIED BY A HUMAN AT A REAL CONSOLE: mouse-driven use of the popover (hover states, wheel scrolling inside a long Publisher list). Nothing here is tier-gated or destructive, so this is the ordinary UI-polish gap, not the elevated-confirmation class.

title: Network Activity: beautify upload/download(/ping) into a proper visual instead of inline text
description: Operator wants upload, download and (if approved, see bd kp0) ping shown in a beautified visual, not the current plain inline examined-list text (speedLine appended to the Looked at: line). Depends partly on kp0s outcome for whether ping is included at all; upload/down alone can be redesigned independently as small stat tiles or a compact sparkline-style widget.
close_reason: Replaced the up/down text fragment (previously just another entry in the 'Looked at:' inline note) with three tiles under the verdict: Download, Upload, and a de-emphasised adapter/link tile carrying the adapter name, Wi-Fi/Wired and signal % when known. Grid is auto-fit minmax(150px,1fr) so it reflows to one column on a narrow window. Adapter name and the two rates were removed from the 'Looked at:' line so the same numbers are not printed twice. Built independent of kp0 as that issue allows - no ping, and the layout takes a fourth tile without rework if that decision later lands. Deliberately did NOT express the rates as a percentage of link speed: linkSpeedBps is the negotiated rate to the router, not the speed of the internet connection behind it, so a percentage would be a confident wrong answer against the wrong denominator. Caught by this project's own test/icon-verify.js while verifying: fa-arrow-down, fa-arrow-up and fa-ethernet were not in the vendored icon set, so all three tiles rendered a blank 1em square with nothing thrown and nothing logged - exactly the failure mode that test exists for. Added the three glyphs to assets/icons.css on the same 24x24/2px grid (55 defined, 55 referenced, 0 missing) and re-captured the panel to confirm they paint. npm test 395/0.

title: Game platform size detection: verify and add GOG Galaxy, Ubisoft Connect, EA App, Battle.net
description: Add-GamePlatformSizes now uses an extensible provider array (GamePlatformSizeProviders) with Steam (live-verified) and Epic (documented format, not live-tested) implemented. GOG Galaxy got real research this session: it does write a per-game goggame-<id>.info JSON file with what looks like a depots array carrying per-depot size fields, matching what a content-manifest download-time format uses - but every source found describes the DOWNLOAD manifest, not confirmed against the actual local post-install file contents on a real machine. Implementing from research alone risks a wrong field name silently attaching a plausible-but-incorrect size to a real game, which is worse than the current unknown-size status quo. Needs a real GOG install to verify field names before writing Get-GogLibrarySizes. Ubisoft Connect and EA App/Origin/Battle.net were not researched at all this session - lower priority, add if a user reports the same unknown-size gap for one of them.
notes: BLOCKED ON HARDWARE, not on effort - checked 2026-08-18. None of the four platforms is installed on this machine: GOG Galaxy, Ubisoft Connect, EA Desktop and Battle.net all absent from their registry keys, and a recursive search for goggame-*.info across C: and D: found zero files. So the exact thing the bead says is required - verifying the real field names in a real post-install goggame-*.info rather than in download-manifest documentation - cannot be done here. Implementing from research alone would attach a plausible-but-wrong size to a real game, which the bead already judged worse than the current honest 'unknown size'. Deferred rather than closed: it becomes a half-hour job the moment any of these is installed on a machine we can read.

title: GPU pills: real AMD/NVIDIA vendor logos blocked on unreliable phys-index-to-vendor correlation
description: Operator wants real AMD/NVIDIA logos on the Task Manager GPU pills instead of generic GPU 0/GPU 1 labels. Two separate problems, only one attempted: (1) trademark/licensing - using the literal AMD/NVIDIA brand marks needs a legitimately licensed source (e.g. Simple Icons, CC0-licensed glyphs explicitly meant for non-endorsement hardware-identification use) rather than freehand SVG authoring; not yet sourced. (2) technical correlation - attempted to resolve phys_N (the GPU Engine perf counter index) to a real vendor via DXGI COM interop (CreateDXGIFactory1/IDXGIFactory1/IDXGIAdapter1.GetDesc1, which returns VendorId and AdapterLuid per adapter - the authoritative source, since the perf counters instance name embeds the same LUID). The interop compiled but returned no usable output when invoked live - IDXGIFactory1 inherits IDXGIObject (4 methods) and IDXGIFactory (5 methods) ahead of EnumAdapters1 in the real vtable, and the attempted interface declared EnumAdapters1 alone as if it were the first slot, which is very likely why it silently failed rather than returning wrong-looking-plausible data (the safer failure mode, but still not working). Full, correct declarations for the inherited interfaces were not attempted due to time and risk (a subtly wrong vtable order does not fail loudly - it either crashes or silently misreads memory through the wrong method, which is a bad trade for a cosmetic feature). Only one GPU (phys_0) had any active instances during testing (the discrete GPU was idle, standard Optimus behavior) so even a working interop could not have been empirically cross-checked against phys_1 without deliberately loading the dGPU first.
design: Options, none attempted yet: (A) redo the DXGI interop correctly, declaring the full IDXGIObject+IDXGIFactory method sets ahead of EnumAdapters1 so the vtable actually lines up - more real interop work, but would be authoritative if done right. (B) Show real vendor names/logos as a static, one-time legend elsewhere (e.g. Health Advisor Graphics card, which already reliably has both names via Win32_VideoController) WITHOUT attaching them to the live per-index percentage numbers, so the honest generic GPU 0/GPU 1 labels stay on the numbers that cannot be safely correlated. (C) Accept generic GPU 0/GPU 1 permanently, matching real Windows Task Managers own precedent for the identical limitation.
notes: SUPERSEDED same session: the array-order best-effort correlation described in the closing reason was replaced before ever shipping. Operator pointed out phys_N is unstable (a hibernated dGPU can vanish from or shift within the perf counters adapter list) and asked to key on a stable id instead. Found one: chrome://gpu (loaded once in a hidden window, parsed via a shadow-DOM-aware walk) reports LUID alongside vendor/name for every adapter, and that LUID is bit-for-bit identical to the one Get-GpuUsageByProcess already reads from the perf counter for the same physical card - verified live. Get-GpuUsageByProcess now returns luidHigh/luidLow per phys_N entry; get-gpu-vendors (main.js) returns luidHigh/luidLow per adapter from chrome://gpu, cached once per process lifetime (not re-queried per sample); renderer matches by LUID equality, not physIndex. Numeric GPU N label still shown alongside any logo - a LUID gpuVendorInfo has never seen (freshly woken GPU, or lookup not yet resolved) falls back to it cleanly.
close_reason: Resolved via a different, more reliable path than the blocked DXGI COM interop attempt: Electron already enumerates every GPU adapter internally for its own rendering (app.getGPUInfo(complete)) and exposes vendorId + deviceString + active per adapter - live-tested and confirmed correct vendor IDs (0x1002=AMD, 0x10DE=NVIDIA) for both real GPUs on the operators machine, no custom native interop needed at all. New get-gpu-vendors IPC handler (main.js) wraps this, filtered to exclude the Microsoft Basic Render Driver software fallback. Real AMD/NVIDIA logos added to assets/icons.css (fa-amd, fa-nvidia) sourced from Simple Icons (CC0-licensed icon files; the marks themselves remain their respective trademark owners, informational hardware-identification use). Correlation to the GPU Engine perf counters phys_N index is still array-order best-effort (no LUID exposed by getGPUInfo to prove it definitively) - the numeric GPU 0/GPU 1 label stays alongside the logo for exactly this reason, documented in code comments. npm test 371/0, npm run verify 174/0, icon-verify 3/0 - all clean.

title: Game platform installs (Steam/Epic/etc) detected with unknown size and incomplete metadata
description: Operator report: Vanish detected GTA 5 as installed but with unknown size. Steam, Epic, and other game platforms manage installs, sizes, caches, and updates independently of a standard Programs-and-Features registry entry - the uninstall registry key for a Steam game typically points at Steams own uninstaller and rarely carries a real EstimatedSize value, unlike a normal MSI/EXE installer. Some real data IS available (Steam library manifests under steamapps/libraryfolders.vdf and appmanifest_<id>.acf carry real install sizes and paths; Epic has a similar per-game manifest under ProgramData/Epic/EpicGamesLauncher/Data/Manifests). Scope: read platform-specific manifests where present to backfill size/path for game entries that are otherwise unknown, rather than relying solely on the generic uninstall-registry scan. Explicitly deferred by the operator until after the current assignment - do not start until asked.
close_reason: Confirmed via the real Steam registry key: Steam DOES still write a normal Programs-and-Features entry per game (name, uninstall string, InstallLocation all correct) - only EstimatedSize is blank, because Steam owns that number, not Windows. Fixed by reading Steams own already-computed size instead of asking Windows for one it never has: Get-SteamLibrarySizes finds every Steam library via steamapps/libraryfolders.vdf (a Steam install can span multiple drives - confirmed on the operators machine, C: and D:SteamLibrary), then each librarys appmanifest_<id>.acf for installdir+SizeOnDisk, keyed by full install path. Add-GamePlatformSizes backfills sizeBytes only when the registry itself reported none and installLocation matches - nothing else about the entry is touched. Live-verified: GTA V Enhanced now reports sizeBytes=103224354965 (was blank), matching Steams own SizeOnDisk exactly. Epic support (Get-EpicManifestSizes, documented .item JSON manifest shape) implemented the same way but NOT live-tested - Epic isnt installed on the machine this was written against. Cost: lazy (only reads library/manifest files when a blank-size entry with a real install location is actually found), full-list scan measured 1209ms (up from ~350ms baseline, one-time per scan, not per-app) - not the recursive folder-size walk that cost Get-UwpApps 10-15s and was removed earlier this session. npm test 371/0, npm run verify 174/0.

title: Audit Mode write-attempt UX: dedicated messaging vs generic error toast
description: Backend fullModeOnly() (main.js:50-69) and renderer guardFullMode() (renderer.js:466-470) do block writes in Audit Mode and do surface something -- guardFullMode's own toast pre-empts most cases, and if that's bypassed the generic per-action error toast picks up the rejection string verbatim. Not literally silent, but the About page disclaimer ('Useful before it is powerful') is a different piece of copy from what a user actually sees mid-action, and the two were never checked against each other. Confirm the guardFullMode toast copy matches what actually explains the block (not just 'try again'), and decide whether it needs a more prominent one-time explainer the first time a write is attempted in Audit Mode, vs relying on the always-visible top banner.
close_reason: Verified rather than changed: guardFullMode()'s toast already states cause (Audit Mode) and remedy (restart as administrator) before any destructive IPC call fires, and every destructive control (including the new Clean All button, zl4) carries data-destructive=true so applyTierLocks() greys it out with a hover tooltip in Audit Mode too - this is already regular UX, not just the About-page disclaimer. No separate one-time explainer added; the always-visible top banner plus per-action toast already cover it without adding a second competing UI surface.

title: Icon audit: five referenced fa-* classes were never defined
description: Closed on sight, recorded because the failure mode is worth keeping: assets/icons.css defines first-party SVG masks, and a class it does not define renders as a 1em blank square with no error and no log entry. fa-lightbulb (every orphaned startup row), fa-clock, fa-location-dot, fa-wifi and fa-arrows-up-down were all live and invisible. No DOM test catches this because the element IS present and IS the right size. test/icon-verify.js now diffs referenced against defined.
close_reason: Fixed in the same commit that found it: all five drawn in assets/icons.css, test/icon-verify.js added to run-all so the next undefined reference fails the build.

title: Stage 13 info-only slice: count installed runtime redistributables
description: 22 separate Visual C++ Redistributable packages measured installed on the operator's machine. The reduced Stage 13 ships as pure information - a read-only count/list on the existing app list, no removal, no PE-import parsing. The removal half needs an import-table cross-reference and stays deferred until the number itself has been in front of users.
acceptance_criteria: The app list states how many redistributable packages are installed and lets the user see them; no uninstall action is offered from this surface.
close_reason:
Shipped 2026-08-18 as information only, which is the reduced Stage 13 scope. scanner.ps1 annotates every uninstall entry with an explicit isRuntime boolean derived from the SharedRuntimePattern it already used for classification, and All Programs gains a 'Runtimes only' toggle with a live count badge beside the existing Components and Windows features toggles.

MEASURED here: 33 shared runtimes of 149 entries (the bead's 22 was Visual C++ alone; the pattern also catches .NET runtimes, WebView2 and DirectX).

WHAT IT ACTUALLY FIXES: these were never hidden - they are classified as components and were always reachable - but with no count and no way to see them as a group, 33 near-identical rows just read as noise inside a list of real programs. The count is on screen before anything is clicked, and it is stated in the list caption whether or not the filter is on, because a number that only appears once you have found the control answers the question too late.

ACCEPTANCE MET, both halves, asserted in test/runtimes-verify.js (11 passed, 0 failed): the app list states how many are installed and lets the user see them, and NO uninstall action is offered from this surface (asserted: 0 of 33 rows carry an uninstall control). The removal half stays deferred - deciding whether a runtime is still needed means reading the import tables of every binary on the machine, and without that 'safe to remove' is a guess that breaks a program which will never say why.

One design trap caught by its own assertion: runtimes ARE components, so isolating them while components are hidden produced an empty table that read as 'you have none'. The toggle now reveals components automatically, and the test asserts the row count equals the runtime count rather than merely being non-zero.

title: Stage 11: SharedDLLs dead-reference cleaner + ghost PnP device sweep
description: Two small Stage 11 items with no issue. (1) SharedDLLs: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\SharedDLLs entries whose path fails Test-Path - dead reference counts, same orphan pattern as the existing cleaners. (2) Ghost PnP devices: 80 devices measured at Status=Unknown, of which 23 are benign VolumeSnapshot records and most of the rest are unplugged peripherals. Rule 24 applies hard here - a ghost restore-point record and a genuinely failed device must not read as the same alarming thing, so classify by class or do not show it.
notes: Same disposition as be8: cheap finding types on the existing scan surface, not a subsystem. Zero space freed. Rule 24 is the real work here - 80 ghost PnP devices of which 23 are benign VolumeSnapshot records, and a ghost snapshot record must never read as alarming as a genuinely failed device.
close_reason:
Shipped 2026-08-18 as one audit-only section ('Dead references and ghost devices'), since neither half is big enough to earn its own row and both answer the same question - what does Windows still have a record of that is not there.

(1) SharedDLLs: values under CurrentVersion\SharedDLLs whose path fails Test-Path after expansion. 0 on this machine, which is itself worth knowing; asserted that any listed entry really is missing from disk.
(2) Ghost PnP devices: 107 found at Status=Unknown.

RULE 24 WAS THE REAL WORK, exactly as the bead predicted, and it is enforced by assertions rather than intent. Every ghost is classified before it is shown - a System Restore bookkeeping record (36 found here, and asserted to SAY that rather than read like broken hardware), a peripheral that is simply not plugged in, a drive that is not attached, or a device Windows cannot see. A further assertion forbids any of them being dressed up as risky: they are all risk=Safe, because they are records, not damage.

Both halves are listed and never offered for removal - they free zero bytes, they need the value-level restore path, and removing a ghost device record can force a driver reinstall on the next plug-in. The note on each finding says which of those applies.

title: Unlocker: select from a list of currently-locked items, not just Browse
description:
Follow-up to the 2026-08-05 Unlocker fix (browse-for-path native picker, replacing manual path typing). The Browse button solves 'I have to type a path' but not the operator's other ask: pick from a list of things already known to be locked, rather than hunting down a path manually.

openUnlockerFor(path) already exists (renderer.js) and pre-fills+auto-searches when triggered from the FLOW-02 locked-item shortcut on the purge summary screen - so contextual pre-fill already happens in that one case. What is missing: a persistent, broader entry point - e.g. surfacing paths already known to be locked from a failed purge/uninstall attempt, or a quick-pick list of the current app's own leftover items mid-wizard, rather than only the single post-purge shortcut.

Needs its own design pass: where does the 'known locked items' list come from (recent failed purges via oplog? the current wizard's leftover tree specifically?), and how does that avoid becoming yet another list the operator has to maintain.
design:
DESIGN PASS 2026-08-16. The bead asked two questions - where does the 'known locked items' list come from, and how does it avoid becoming another list the operator has to maintain. Both answered, with a third finding that has to be settled first.

FINDING, and it is the blocker: THERE IS NO SOURCE ON DISK TODAY.
- main.js's oplog records for quarantine/cleaner-purge carry COUNTS only: lib/vault.js:58-62 logs { requested, quarantined, failed: countFailed(entry) }. Not one failed PATH, and not one reason.
- The per-item failures DO survive in the vault manifest - entry.files[].status === 'failed' (countFailed, lib/vault.js:97) - but ONLY when the purge partially succeeded. lib/vault.js:51 adds the manifest entry only when result.quarantinedCount > 0, so a purge where EVERY item was locked writes nothing anywhere.
- The FLOW-02 shortcut (renderer/wizard.js:523) works only because 'problems' is still in memory on that screen. Navigate away and the knowledge is gone.
So 'surface paths already known to be locked' cannot be built by reading what exists. Something has to start recording them.

WHERE THE LIST COMES FROM - recommendation: paths VANISH ITSELF failed to remove with a lock reason. Nothing else on the machine knows that set, which is what makes it worth building. isLockFailure() (renderer/wizard.js:534) is already the classifier and already drives the per-item shortcut; the change is persisting what it classifies instead of discarding it.

REJECTED, with reasons, so this is not re-litigated:
(a) A system-wide 'what is locked right now' scan. That is Resource Monitor's Associated Handles search and Process Explorer's Find Handle, both of which the operator already has, and CLAUDE.md's standard is written against exactly this. It also costs a full handle enumeration to answer a question nobody asked.
(b) The current wizard's leftover tree as a quick-pick. That lists items NOT known to be locked, so it invites the operator to check paths at random - the opposite of the feature. The one leftover that IS known locked already has its button.

HOW IT AVOIDS BECOMING A LIST TO MAINTAIN - it prunes itself, and every rule is a fact rather than a policy:
- the path no longer exists -> drop it (it was removed some other way);
- a later removal of that path succeeds -> drop it;
- list-lockers returns zero holders when opened -> say 'nothing is holding this now' and drop it, rather than showing an empty result;
- bounded ring, newest first, ~50 entries;
- one visible Clear action.
Each row shows the path, what tried to remove it, when, and the reason - the same four facts the failure screen showed at the time, which is what makes the entry legible a week later.

WHAT IT TOUCHES: a new small store in lib/store.js (lockedPathsPath(), same readJson/writeJsonAtomic pattern as networkHoldPath); a write where lock failures are currently only rendered; a quick-pick list in the unlock modal (index.html:552 opens it empty today); reuse of openUnlockerFor(path), which already pre-fills and auto-searches.

OPEN DECISION FOR THE OPERATOR, and the reason this is not already built: this adds a new piece of PERSISTED STATE about the user's machine - a record of paths that failed to delete, kept on disk across sessions. Every other store in this app is either the vault (which the user opted into per action) or settings. This one accumulates quietly. It is defensible - it is the user's own failed actions, it prunes itself, and it never leaves the device (INV-4) - but it is a privacy-shaped call, not a UI call, and it should be made deliberately rather than discovered later in a data directory.
notes: Design pass done 2026-08-16, implementation NOT started - deliberately. The design is settled and the rejected alternatives are recorded; what is left is the one operator decision named above (a new persisted record of failed-delete paths) plus the build. Ready to implement the moment that is answered.

title: Windows Update: a legible list and a one-click handoff, not a rollback engine
description:
UN-CUT and rescoped 2026-08-12. I cut this as redundant; the operator corrected the premise and they are right: Windows CAN roll updates back, but the process and interface are hostile - Settings > Windows Update > Update history > Uninstall updates, several clicks deep, a bare KB list with no indication of what any of them is, no install dates surfaced usefully, and no explanation of what removing one costs you.

So the redundancy was never the rollback - it was ME proposing to reimplement wusa/DISM. That part stays cut. What we build is the part Windows does badly:

BUILD (ours, and small):
  - A legible list. Get-HotFix + DISM /Online /Get-Packages, both READ-ONLY, joined into one view: KB number, what kind of update it is (security / cumulative / driver / .NET), when it was installed, and whether it is removable at all (many cumulative updates are not, and Windows tells you this only by failing).
  - The one piece of judgement nobody offers: 'installed 3 days ago' next to 'this machine started misbehaving 3 days ago'. That is the actual reason anyone opens this screen, and it is the same question zrw's snapshot diff answers for installers. Cross-reference the two once both exist.
  - An honest cost line per update, especially for security updates.

DO NOT BUILD (this is the redundant half, still cut):
  - No removal engine. The Remove button shells out to the Windows mechanism that already exists and lets IT do the work and own the outcome: wusa.exe /uninstall /kb:NNNNNNN for MSU-packaged updates (which shows Windows' own uninstall UI and its own restart prompt), or open Settings' Uninstall Updates page directly (ms-settings:windowsupdate-history) when the package is CBS-only and wusa cannot take it.
  - No vault entry, no restore manifest, no progress UI of our own. We do not own this removal and must not imply we can reverse it - Windows Update reinstalls the update, that is the restore path, and the UI should say exactly that.
  - No auto-selection, no 'clean up old updates' bulk action, ever.

This is the same shape as the native-uninstaller handoff the wizard already does: Vanish finds it, explains it, and lets the vendor's own tool perform the destructive act.

Rule note: MANDATORY-REVIEW-GATE still applies, and is trivially satisfied because the user ends up in Windows' own confirmation UI.
design: Read-only until the handoff. The entire feature is a query, a join, and a ShellExecute - if it grows a removal code path of its own, it has become the thing we cut.
acceptance_criteria: Every listed update shows type, install date and removability; the Remove action launches the Windows mechanism rather than performing the removal; nothing in the UI claims Vanish can restore an update it did not remove.
notes: PARKED 2026-08-06 by operator directive ('implode the fluff, build a robust software'). This stage was scoped during a session that added new roadmap surface while the ALREADY-SHIPPED surfaces were substantially broken (see epic vanish-uninstaller-7oo). Scoping was sound; the sequencing was not. Do not start this until epic 7oo's P0 children are closed against real data. Rule 16's Core-VM gate still applies on top of that.
close_reason:
Shipped 2026-08-18 as a Health Advisor section. BUILT the half Windows does badly; the removal half stays cut, and the test asserts that rather than trusting it - the engine function never INVOKES a remover (no call operator on wusa, no Start-Process wusa, no Remove-WindowsPackage / Remove-Package / Uninstall-WindowsFeature / Remove-WindowsCapability), and the only mention of wusa in the whole function is the command string it reports for the user to run themselves.

WHAT IT SHOWS: KB number, what KIND of update it is (security / cumulative / driver / .NET / Defender / optional component / servicing stack / hotfix), when it was installed, and a cost line per row saying what removing it would actually mean - which is the judgement nobody offers. Security updates name the risk; servicing-stack updates say Windows will refuse rather than explain; cumulative ones say you are rolling back months rather than a day; drivers point at Device Manager, which keeps the previous version.

TWO SOURCES, and the missing one is REPORTED rather than hidden: Get-HotFix (works unelevated, 5 rows here) plus DISM /Online /Get-Packages (Full Mode only - unelevated Windows exits 740). Unelevated the payload carries dismAvailable=false and a sentence explaining that the list is short because DISM was refused, which the test asserts. Elevated: 194 rows, 189 of them component-store. Superseded revisions are dropped - they are history the user cannot act on and would triple the list.

THE DATES WERE THE REAL WORK, and the first implementation got them wrong. DISM emits install times in the machine's short-date form; measured here culture en-IN, dd-MM-yyyy, confirmed against 280 samples where field one reaches 28 and field two never exceeds 12. A bare [datetime] cast produced dates FOUR MONTHS IN THE FUTURE at the top of a list sorted by date. Convert-UpdateInstallTime now parses with the current culture then explicit formats, and REJECTS any result in the future - an update cannot have been installed tomorrow, so a future date is proof the parse failed. It returns null plus a reason instead. Fixing it also recovered 92 real dates (110 dated, up from 18). 84 rows carry no date at all because Windows never recorded one, each with that reason attached, and the count is surfaced so a mostly-blank column reads as Windows not recording rather than Vanish not looking. Straight c0y.

The handoff is a dialog stating 'wusa.exe /uninstall /kb:N' and offering to open Settings' own update history. It says plainly that Vanish does not remove updates and could not put one back.

test/updates-verify.js: 26 passed 0 failed unelevated AND 26 passed 0 failed elevated, so both source paths are covered. The stub fixture carries the three shapes that can go wrong rather than the easy one - a dated update, a row with no recorded date, and a component-store package with no KB number (which correctly offers no handoff, since there is no number to hand off).

title: Stage 16: Orphaned Firewall Rule sweep
description:
Standard-tier feature, scoped 2026-08-05 while expanding what Vanish sees/lists/rectifies. Full spec: docs/roadmap.md Stage 16.

Distinct from the Firewall Controller cut from Stage 7 -- that was about judging live processes as 'suspicious' (Rule 6 boundary, still cut, unchanged). This is pure path-existence: does the program a firewall rule references still exist on disk. Same orphan-detection pattern already used for SharedDLLs (Stage 11) and fonts (Stage 12).

Measured on the operator's machine 2026-08-05: 659 total firewall rules, 48 reference a program path that no longer exists once environment variables are expanded. First measurement pass got this wrong -- Test-Path doesn't expand %SystemRoot%-style variables and flagged 295 false positives against live Windows system binaries before being corrected. The real 48 split into dead OS-feature rules (Windows Media Center's ehome\*, removed from Windows years ago; P2P Collaboration Foundation, deprecated), a temp installer's leftover rule, and rules pointing at a since-moved/uninstalled third-party app.

Implementation: Get-NetFirewallRule + Get-NetFirewallApplicationFilter, [Environment]::ExpandEnvironmentVariables on the Program path, then Test-Path. Quarantine-first per Rule 2 (export before removal, not a bare Remove-NetFirewallRule). Per Rule 24, label each finding by why it's dead (removed OS feature / uninstalled third-party app / leftover installer temp path), not a bare 'orphaned' list. Needs elevation for the write path; read/list can run in Audit Mode.

Blocked on: Core tier VM-tested (Rule 16) before it can release, same as every other Standard-tier stage -- design/implementation work is not blocked, only shipping is.

Also considered and rejected in the same pass: UWP/MSIX leftover package-data audit (Packages folders with no matching installed AppxPackage). Measured 14 of 144 folders orphaned, only 25.4MB total, one real item over 1MB. Not worth a dedicated feature at this size -- LEAVE-ALONE per Stage 14's tiering principle, re-measure later if it ever shows up bigger.
acceptance_criteria: Scan lists firewall rules whose Program path fails Test-Path after environment-variable expansion, each labeled with a plain-language reason (removed OS feature / uninstalled app / leftover installer). A planted orphaned rule (fake program path) is found, quarantined (exported before removal), removed, and restored from the vault; restore is verified by the rule reappearing in Get-NetFirewallRule. No removal path exists without a restore/export step.
notes: Kept as a cheap finding type on the existing scan surface, demoted to P3. Nothing else does firewall-rule orphan detection, so it is not redundant - but it frees ZERO disk space and fixes no user-visible symptom (48 dead rules of 659 measured). Ship it when the scan surface is already open, never as its own project.
close_reason:
Shipped 2026-08-18 as an audit-only finding type on the existing cleaner surface. Find-OrphanFirewallRules walks Get-NetFirewallApplicationFilter, expands the Program path with ExpandEnvironmentVariables and then Test-Paths it. Measured here: 56 dead rules out of the machine's full rule set, classified into three reasons that are all really present - 'a Windows feature that no longer ships' (Peer to Peer Collaboration Foundation, Media Center Extenders), 'a rule an installer left behind in a temp folder', and 'a program that is no longer on this PC'.

THE MEASUREMENT TRAP the bead recorded is pinned by an assertion rather than a comment: no rule whose program DOES exist may be listed (0 false positives), which is exactly what the first 2026-08-05 pass got wrong when Test-Path failed to expand %SystemRoot% and flagged 295 live Windows binaries. A second assertion forbids showing an unexpanded %VARIABLE% path to the user at all.

Rule 24 honoured: every rule says WHICH kind of dead it is, asserted, not just that it is dead.

AUDIT ONLY, and the note on every finding says so: removing a rule means deleting a registry VALUE under FirewallPolicy\FirewallRules, which needs the value-level export/restore path the PATH cleaner uses (Set-PathEntries) rather than the key-level one the vault offers. Vanish will not delete what it cannot put back.

title: Stage 15: Bandwidth diagnostics panel + Game/Stream Mode toggle
description:
Standard-tier feature, scoped 2026-08-05 from the Stage 7 disposition after the operator asked for network oversight to keep gaming/streaming from getting starved. Full spec: docs/roadmap.md Stage 15.

Scope boundary (binding, not just current-phase): no real-time per-app packet-level QoS -- that needs a kernel-mode WFP callout driver, a categorically different risk class than anything else in this codebase (driver signing, BSOD blast radius, new privileged attack surface). Permanently out of scope, not deferred. Also cannot fix LAN-level contention from another device -- that's a router problem, out of this app's reach; the panel should say so rather than imply otherwise.

Two parts:
1. Bandwidth panel (read-only): Get-NetTCPConnection/Get-NetUDPEndpoint grouped by OwningProcess, cross-referenced to Get-Process, remote address resolved best-effort. System-wide throughput from Get-NetAdapterStatistics deltas. Per Rule 9, ships as active-connections + system-wide throughput only -- true per-process byte-rate needs an ETW consumer, that is a separate, separately-justified v2.
2. Game/Stream Mode toggle: operator manually picks the process(es) to prioritize (no auto-detect heuristic for v1, matches Stage 4's manual-input philosophy). On enable: throttle Delivery Optimization, throttle/pause BITS, raise selected process priority class, tag selected traffic via New-NetQosPolicy DSCP marking (documented as router/ISP-dependent, no guarantee). On disable: revert every setting touched, same schema-rule-5 pattern as startupMode.

Explicitly cut, not part of this issue: Firewall Controller and general per-app Network Inspector (IP resolution as a security surface) -- Rule 6 boundary, unchanged.

Blocked on: Core tier VM-tested (Rule 16) before it can release, same as every other Standard-tier stage -- design/implementation work is not blocked, only shipping is.
design:
THREE MODELS (operator review 2026-08-07). Bandwidth is a volume problem, ping is a queue problem; conflating them is why network optimizers have their reputation. The biggest lever for ping is the same lever as for bandwidth - your own background traffic is usually your own bufferbloat - so this is one set of levers described honestly twice, not two features.

MODEL A, secure bandwidth. Answers 'my download crawls when Windows is busy'. Levers: pause BITS, cap Delivery Optimization, suspend named consumers, hold until switched off. Says: 'Windows Update paused. 3 transfers held. Nothing else changed.' Cannot give an app more than the link carries - it clears the lane, it does not widen the road. DECISIVE: the actions conclusively remove a competitor and the effect is observable in adapter throughput.

MODEL B, protect ping. Answers 'my game spikes when someone else streams'. Levers: stop this PC filling the queue, DSCP-mark the chosen app, disable NIC power saving, say when Wi-Fi is the cause. Says: 'This PC is no longer adding to the queue. Spikes left are not from here.' Cannot touch another device's traffic - that queue is in the router. NOT DECISIVE: DSCP only helps if the path honours it, and the dominant cause is often a device Vanish cannot see. So A reports what it DID; B reports what it RULED OUT.

MODEL C, best available. Both sets applied together, observed before/during/after, every setting reverted on exit, and it names what it could not reach. Cannot promise a number.

FOURTH OUTCOME, the one nobody ships: any model may end in 'nothing on this machine is the problem'. Say that plainly, show what was examined, point at router QoS - instead of applying five settings and implying they helped.

MEASUREMENT, and how it lands on INV-4: Model A needs throughput only (Get-NetAdapterStatistics deltas) - local, free, no network I/O, no invariant touched. Model B needs RTT under load vs idle, and the cheapest honest source is the DEFAULT GATEWAY: stays on the LAN, contacts no third party. By the letter of INV-4 that is still runtime network I/O, so it is an operator decision, not something to slip in - but it is categorically different from calling speedtest.net.

BUILD ORDER: (1) attribution panel, no network I/O, useful alone; (2) suppression + guaranteed full revert - the real value and the testable part; (3) latency diagnosis, only with the gateway-RTT carve-out approved; (4) DSCP marking last, labelled conditional because it may do nothing.

COPY RULE, testable: the panel states what it changed and what it observed, and never states a delta as a causal claim. A test can fail any percentage-improvement string in this surface, the same way the copy tests assert intent rather than exact prose. Banned: 'up to 40% faster', 'connection grade B+', 'optimized for gaming', 'ping improved by 22ms', 'boost enabled'.
acceptance_criteria: Bandwidth panel lists active TCP/UDP connections grouped by owning process with resolved remote host and system-wide adapter throughput -- no per-process byte-rate claimed. Game/Stream Mode toggle: operator selects target process(es), enabling throttles Delivery Optimization + BITS, raises target priority class, and applies a DSCP QoS policy; disabling reverts every one of those settings back to its prior state, verified by a settings round-trip test. No kernel driver, no per-app real-time packet shaping, no firewall control, no per-app IP/threat display shipped under this issue.
notes: NARROWED 2026-08-12. The read-only bandwidth panel is redundant - Task Manager and Resource Monitor both show per-process network already, and Vanish's own Network Activity panel (bfh.1, shipped) covers attribution. Cut that half. The part nobody else offers is the HOLD (bfh.2): pausing background transfers with a guaranteed way back. bfh.2 is already built and only needs its elevated confirmation, so this parent should not carry panel-expansion scope any more.

title: TASK-16: Multi-user hive sweep + ownership elevator (SHOULD)
description: Phase 4. Full spec: docs/planning/05-implementation-plan.md TASK-16 (context manifest, steps, verify, done-when). Read ONLY the context manifest listed there. Deviation protocol binding.
close_reason: TASK-16 partially done (SHOULD). REQ-17 multi-user profile sweep implemented: enumerates ProfileList, skips the current user, service accounts and already-loaded hives, reg-loads each inactive NTUSER.DAT under HKU\VanishProfile_*, scans Software for a caller-supplied keyword, and unloads every mounted hive in a finally with a GC flush first (NFR-07). Requires a keyword by design - without one it proposes nothing rather than listing every vendor key. Verified elevated via test/phase4-verify.ps1: no hive mounted before, none left mounted after, including on the empty-keyword path. REQ-19 ownership elevator is implemented in the engine (Grant-VanishOwnership: takeown + icacls to Administrators, invoked per item only when the caller passes allowOwnershipElevation and the move failed with an access error, recorded as aclElevated in the manifest row) but is NOT yet surfaced in the wizard UI as a per-item offer, and its acceptance test (quarantining a TrustedInstaller-owned file) has NOT been run. Filing that remainder as its own issue rather than claiming it.

title: TASK-09: Watchdog suspension (SHOULD, blocked on OPEN-01)
description: Phase 2. Full spec: docs/planning/05-implementation-plan.md TASK-09 (context manifest, steps, verify, done-when). Read ONLY the context manifest listed there. Deviation protocol binding.
close_reason: TASK-09 done (SHOULD, delivered): NtSuspendProcess/NtResumeProcess via Add-Type per OPEN-01, process tree discovered through Win32_Process BFS, handles held open from discovery through the whole freeze so a recycled PID cannot be resumed or killed by mistake. ProcessFreezer implements IDisposable and Unlock-Path calls Dispose() in a finally, so the thaw is guaranteed including on error. Terminate() resumes before terminating. Verified elevated via test/phase2-verify.ps1 with a real watchdog pair: CONTROL case proves killing the holder alone lets the watchdog respawn it; the suspend-then-unlock path leaves the file free with no respawn; and no test process is left suspended afterwards. Undocumented ntdll export retained deliberately per OPEN-01 - do not 'fix' it back to SuspendThread.

comments.author: QuantumMonkey
comments.text:
OPEN-01 FINDINGS (Gemini Pro, 2026-07-11):
Recommended mechanism: NtSuspendProcess/NtResumeProcess (ntdll), process tree discovery via Get-CimInstance Win32_Process.
Why: undocumented but the exact API Sysinternals Process Explorer uses; stable across Win10/11; atomic kernel-level whole-process suspension. Documented SuspendThread+Toolhelp32 alternative has a TOCTOU race (threads spawn during enumeration).
Code sketch: scratch/NtSuspendProcess-Sketch.ps1 (Antigravity scratch - NOT merged; Sonnet reimplements per spec gate).
Failure modes: Access Denied on protected/higher-priv processes (mitigated: Vanish runs elevated); PID reuse during discovery (mitigated: hold handles open after discovery).
Resume guarantee: C# class implements IDisposable storing opened handles; PS wraps in try/finally { $suspender.Dispose() } so resume+handle-close always runs.
Confidence 9/10; residual risk = MS deprecating the ntdll export (improbable - would break debuggers/anti-cheat/security tooling).

title: About page: decide whether to keep full tech-stack + data-folder-path disclosure
description: renderer.js:1052-1079 About panel reveals exact Electron/Chromium/Node versions, GitHub repo URL, and the full local Data folder filesystem path (info.dataDir) verbatim. Open product question, not a bug: does full version disclosure or the raw local path create any downside for an open-source, no-network desktop tool? Record the decision and reasoning (likely: keep -- no network exposure, matches project's transparency ethos -- but consider making the data-folder line a 'reveal in Explorer' action instead of raw text) rather than changing silently.
close_reason: Decision: keep full tech-stack + data-folder disclosure on About. Reasoning: Vanish has zero network I/O (asserted by test/network-verify.ps1), so exact Electron/Chromium/Node versions and the local data-folder path are never exposed to anyone but the person already sitting at the machine looking at its own About panel - there is no remote attacker this could inform. Matches the project's stated transparency ethos ('never pretends it can do something it cannot'). Not changed: the data-folder line could become a clickable 'reveal in Explorer' action to match Settings' existing set-open-data button, but that is a UX nicety, not a disclosure-risk fix - left for a future pass, not bundled into this one.

title: Stage 10 (Extended): WMI/DCOM orphans, event log channels, offsets DB
description: Extended tier, no committed timeline, no issue until now. DCOM/WMI namespace cleanup carries promptgate Rule 17: mandatory per-item review gate, auto-deletion permanently disabled by default, quarantine manifest before any removal. Also here: orphaned EventLog channel registrations, and the crowdsourced offsets JSON for mapping atypical directories (.config, .toolcache, .unity3d) that do not match application names. Waits on the clean-VM pass (0xt) like everything else Standard-and-above.
close_reason:
Cut as redundant, per operator direction 2026-08-12: 'solve problems that are not solved... dont build redundant nonsense'.

ag0 (Windows Update rollback): Windows Settings > Installed Updates already does this, using the EXACT mechanisms this issue specified - wusa.exe /uninstall and DISM /Remove-Package. Vanish would be a second front-end on the same API with no added capability: the vault cannot make a removed security update reversible in any way Windows' own reinstall does not already, and the issue's own binding requirement (MANDATORY-REVIEW-GATE, no auto tier) means it cannot even be faster. The genuinely unserved question nearby is 'which update correlates with when this machine changed', which is zrw's snapshot diff, not a rollback button.

0ng (Driver Store sweeper): pnputil ships with Windows and Disk Cleanup already offers 'Device driver packages'. Worse, the issue documents that INV-1 CANNOT be honoured here - pnputil /delete-driver destroys the FileRepository copy, so a restore manifest would be a promise the vault cannot keep. Building a removal path that breaks the app's own foundational invariant to duplicate a built-in tool is the definition of what we are cutting. The audit-only half already ships (cleaner-scan cleaner=drivers, removable=false) and is the honest version.

dfe (WMI/DCOM orphans, event log channels, offsets DB): P4, no committed timeline, near-zero user-visible value, and Rule 17 would gate it behind mandatory per-item review anyway. Nothing here is a problem a user has ever reported having.

None of these are deleted work - each is recoverable from bd history if the reasoning changes.
